questions.passage:
The following text is from a 1911 short story. Mrs. Pell has just moved from a city apartment to a farmhouse.

The silence was the first thing. In the city there had always been something: a streetcar, a neighbor's radio through the wall, footsteps on the stair. Here the quiet had a weight to it, and for the first week Mrs. Pell slept badly, waking at every creak of the old house as if it had spoken her name. By the second week she had begun, without quite noticing, to listen for the creaks, and to feel that the house was keeping her company.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the main idea of the text?
choices: Mrs. Pell regrets leaving the city and plans to return.
Mrs. Pell gradually comes to feel at home in a place that at first unsettled her.
The farmhouse is in poor repair and needs extensive work.
Mrs. Pell's neighbors in the city were noisy and inconsiderate.
questions.explanation: The text traces a change: the silence first keeps Mrs. Pell awake, then by the second week she listens for the creaks and feels the house is 'keeping her company.' Choice A contradicts that shift; C and D are details, not the point.

questions.passage: The Kumbh Mela, a Hindu pilgrimage held in rotation among four cities in India, draws tens of millions of participants over several weeks. Managing a temporary city of that size requires planning on an enormous scale: in 2019, organizers laid more than 300 kilometers of roads, built over 120,000 toilets, and set up a network of hospitals and lost-and-found centers, all on floodplain land that is submerged for much of the year. Urban planners have begun studying the event as a model for building infrastructure quickly and then removing it without a trace.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Floodplain land is unsuitable for permanent construction.
The Kumbh Mela is the largest religious gathering in the world.
The scale of temporary infrastructure built for the Kumbh Mela has made it a subject of interest to urban planners.
Organizers of the Kumbh Mela struggle to provide adequate sanitation for participants.
questions.explanation: The text lists the infrastructure built for the event and ends with planners studying it as a model. Choice B overstates what the text says; A is background; D is contradicted by the figures given.

questions.passage: Some economists argue that the true cost of a product includes 'externalities,' harms borne by people who neither make nor buy it. A factory that pollutes a river, for instance, shifts part of its cost onto everyone downstream. Because these costs do not appear on any price tag, markets tend to produce more of such goods than would be socially ideal. Proposals to tax pollution are one attempt to fold externalities back into the price, so that buyers and sellers, rather than bystanders, pay for the harm.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Pollution taxes have proven ineffective at reducing the output of factories.
Buyers are generally unaware of the environmental harm caused by the products they purchase.
Economists disagree about whether externalities exist.
Markets overproduce goods whose full costs fall on people outside the transaction, and pollution taxes aim to correct this.
questions.explanation: The text defines externalities, explains why they lead to overproduction, and presents pollution taxes as a remedy. Choice A is not supported; C mischaracterizes the text, which presents externalities as an accepted concept; B is not discussed.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1892 short story "The Yellow Wallpaper." The narrator has been confined to a room to rest.

I'm really getting quite fond of the big room, all but that horrid paper. Out of one window I can see the garden, those mysterious deep-shaded arbors, the riotous old-fashioned flowers, and bushes and gnarly trees. Out of another I get a lovely view of the bay and a little private wharf belonging to the estate. There is a beautiful shaded lane that runs down there from the house. I always fancy I see people walking in these numerous paths and arbors, but John has cautioned me not to give way to fancy in the least.
questions.stem: According to the text, what is true about the narrator?
choices: She finds the wallpaper more pleasant than the view outside.
She has asked John to remove the wallpaper.
She is not permitted to leave the estate.
She has been advised to restrain her imagination.
questions.explanation: The narrator says John 'has cautioned me not to give way to fancy in the least,' that is, to restrain her imagination. Choice C goes beyond the text; A is reversed (she dislikes the paper); B is not mentioned.

questions.passage: Engineers have long assumed that the intricate tunnels of termite mounds are ventilation systems that keep the colony cool. Measurements inside mounds in Namibia, however, showed that the interior temperature barely changes across the day even as the outside air swings by 20 degrees Celsius, which cooling by airflow alone could not explain. Instead, the researchers found that the mounds work primarily as gas exchangers: daily changes in outside temperature drive air back and forth through the tunnels, flushing out carbon dioxide and drawing in oxygen, much as a lung does.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Measurements in Namibia suggest that termite mounds function less as cooling systems than as devices for exchanging gases.
Engineers have been unable to measure conditions inside termite mounds.
Termite mounds are built primarily to regulate temperature rather than to exchange gases.
Termite colonies in Namibia are exposed to larger temperature swings than colonies elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The text sets up the old assumption (ventilation for cooling), gives evidence against it, and states the new conclusion: the mounds are 'primarily gas exchangers.' Choice C reverses this; D and B are not supported.

questions.passage: Historians of reading once assumed that the spread of silent reading in medieval Europe reflected a change in readers' minds, a new capacity for private thought. Paul Saenger's study of manuscripts suggests a more mechanical cause. Ancient and early medieval Latin was written without spaces between words, which made texts difficult to decode without sounding them out. Only after Irish and English scribes began separating words in the seventh and eighth centuries did silent reading become widespread, first in monasteries and later among lay readers. The habit of the mind, Saenger argues, followed the habit of the page.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Monasteries discouraged reading aloud in order to preserve silence.
Saenger argues that a change in how texts were written, rather than a change in mental capacity, made silent reading widespread.
Irish and English scribes were more skilled than their counterparts elsewhere in Europe.
Silent reading was impossible before the seventh century.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts the older explanation (a change in minds) with Saenger's (word spacing on the page) and concludes that 'the habit of the mind followed the habit of the page.' Choice D is too absolute; C and A are not claimed.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Herman Melville's 1851 novel Moby-Dick. The narrator, Ishmael, explains why he goes to sea.

Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people's hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence?
choices: It presents going to sea as the narrator's alternative to a more desperate response to his low spirits.
It reveals that the narrator is planning an act of violence against others.
It explains that the narrator earns his living as a soldier.
It suggests that the narrator's gloomy moods are brief and easily cured.
questions.explanation: 'Pistol and ball' alludes to suicide; going to sea is Ishmael's 'substitute' for it, that is, his way of coping with despair. Choice B misreads the hat-knocking as a real plan; C and D are not supported.

questions.passage: Before refrigeration, ice was harvested from frozen lakes in New England each winter, packed in sawdust, and shipped as far as India and the Caribbean. The trade, begun by the Boston merchant Frederic Tudor in 1806, was ridiculed at first; newspapers joked that he was shipping a product that would be gone before it arrived. By the 1850s, however, insulated icehouses and faster ships had made the business profitable, and 'Boston ice' had become a luxury in cities around the world.
questions.stem: According to the text, how did the public initially react to Tudor's ice trade?
choices: With mockery, because the ice seemed likely to melt in transit.
With indifference, because refrigeration already existed.
With alarm, because harvesting ice damaged the lakes.
With enthusiasm, because ice was scarce in warm climates.
questions.explanation: The text says the trade 'was ridiculed at first; newspapers joked' that the ice would be gone before it arrived. The other choices contradict the text or add unsupported claims.

questions.passage: Many people assume that a bilingual child learns each language more slowly than a monolingual child learns one. Studies of vocabulary size support this only if the two languages are counted separately: a bilingual four-year-old typically knows fewer words in English than a monolingual peer. When words from both languages are counted together, however, the bilingual child's total vocabulary is usually the same size or larger. The apparent delay, in other words, is an artifact of measuring only half of what the child knows.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The impression that bilingual children learn language slowly comes from counting only one of their languages.
Studies of vocabulary size in young children are unreliable.
Bilingual children should be tested only in their stronger language.
Bilingual children typically know more English words than monolingual children do.
questions.explanation: The text argues the 'apparent delay' is 'an artifact of measuring only half of what the child knows.' Choice D is contradicted; B and C go beyond what the text claims.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Kate Chopin's 1899 novel The Awakening.

The voice of the sea is seductive; never ceasing, whispering, clamoring, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander for a spell in abysses of solitude; to lose itself in mazes of inward contemplation. The voice of the sea speaks to the soul. The touch of the sea is sensuous, enfolding the body in its soft, close embrace.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It lists the dangers of the sea and then its pleasures.
It presents a claim about the sea and then offers evidence against it.
It compares the sea to a person and then to a maze.
It describes the sea's effect on the mind and then its effect on the body.
questions.explanation: The first two sentences concern the sea's voice and the 'soul' and 'inward contemplation'; the last concerns its 'touch' on 'the body.' No claim is refuted (B); the maze is a passing image, not a structural turn (C); no dangers are listed (A).

questions.passage: In 1900 the mathematician Emmy Noether began attending lectures at the University of Erlangen, where women could sit in only with each professor's permission and could not formally enroll. When the rule changed she enrolled, completed a doctorate in 1907, and then worked for years without pay because the university would not hire a woman. When David Hilbert tried to bring her to Göttingen in 1915, colleagues objected that soldiers returning from the war would not tolerate learning from a woman; Hilbert replied that the faculty was not a bathhouse. Her theorem linking symmetries to conservation laws, published in 1918, remains one of the foundations of modern physics.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that Noether's theorem was more important than Hilbert's own work.
To explain the mathematical content of Noether's 1918 theorem.
To describe the obstacles Noether faced in her career and the significance of the work she produced despite them.
To criticize the University of Göttingen for its treatment of returning soldiers.
questions.explanation: Each sentence describes a barrier (permission to attend, no pay, colleagues' objections) and the last states the lasting importance of her work. Choice A makes a comparison the text does not; B and D describe things the text does not do.

questions.passage: Octopuses have three hearts. Two of them pump blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen; the third pumps that oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Oddly, the third heart stops beating whenever the octopus swims, which is one reason these animals prefer to crawl along the seafloor: swimming leaves them quickly exhausted.
questions.stem: According to the text, why do octopuses tend to crawl rather than swim?
choices: Their bodies are too heavy to remain suspended in water.
Their gills cannot absorb oxygen while they are swimming.
Crawling allows them to hide from predators more effectively.
Swimming causes one of their hearts to stop, leaving them tired.
questions.explanation: The text states that the third heart 'stops beating whenever the octopus swims,' so 'swimming leaves them quickly exhausted.' The other explanations are not given in the text.

questions.passage: Textile historians have debated why the elaborate patterns of Andean khipus, knotted cords used by the Inca to record information, vary so much from one region to another. Sabine Hyland's fieldwork in the village of San Juan de Collata suggests one answer. Villagers there preserve two khipus that they describe as letters, and they identify each cord's color and fiber (alpaca, llama, or vicuña) as meaningful. If Hyland is right that these features encode sounds rather than numbers, regional differences in khipus may reflect differences in local languages rather than in accounting practice.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Textile historians have reached agreement about the purpose of khipus.
Khipus were used only to record numerical information.
Hyland's research suggests that some khipus may have recorded language, which could explain their regional variation.
The villagers of San Juan de Collata no longer understand the khipus they preserve.
questions.explanation: The text presents a debate about regional variation and Hyland's proposed answer: the cords may encode sounds, so variation may track local languages. B is contradicted by the possibility raised; D is contradicted (villagers identify the features as meaningful); A is contradicted by 'have debated.'

questions.passage:
The following text is from an 1816 novel. Louisa has just persuaded her younger friend Kitty to refuse a marriage proposal from a farmer.

Louisa was not sorry to have the matter settled. A year ago she would have called it a fair match for Kitty, perhaps the best Kitty could hope for; but a year ago Kitty had not been her particular friend, and a farmer's wife could hardly remain so. That she had steered the girl's answer she did not deny to herself, and she felt, faintly, that it had been wrong to do it. But she could not bring herself to regret it. The thing was done, and done by her, and she was glad.
questions.stem: Based on the text, which statement best describes Louisa's attitude toward Kitty's refusal?
choices: She is indifferent to it because she regards the matter as Kitty's alone.
She regrets it because she now thinks the match would have been a good one.
She acknowledges that it was wrong of her to bring it about but is nonetheless pleased with the outcome.
She is troubled by it because she believes Kitty loved the farmer.
questions.explanation: Louisa 'felt, faintly, that it had been wrong' yet 'could not bring herself to regret it' and 'was glad.' Choice B reverses her current view of the match; D and A are not supported.

questions.passage: Sourdough bread rises without commercial yeast because its starter, a mixture of flour and water left to ferment, hosts wild yeasts and bacteria. The bacteria produce lactic and acetic acids, which give the bread its tang and also slow the growth of mold, so that a sourdough loaf keeps longer than one made with ordinary yeast. Bakers sometimes maintain a single starter for decades by feeding it fresh flour every day.
questions.stem: According to the text, what is one effect of the acids produced in a sourdough starter?
choices: They help the bread resist mold.
They cause the bread to rise more quickly.
They allow the starter to be stored without feeding.
They kill the wild yeasts in the starter.
questions.explanation: The text says the acids 'slow the growth of mold, so that a sourdough loaf keeps longer.' None of the other effects are stated.

questions.passage: A high school biology teacher hypothesizes that students retain more from a lab activity when they predict the result before running the experiment than when they simply follow the procedure.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the teacher's hypothesis?
choices: Students' quiz scores were higher for labs conducted in the morning than for those conducted after lunch.
Students who wrote a prediction before a lab scored higher on a quiz about that lab two weeks later than students who did not.
Students reported enjoying labs more than lectures regardless of how the labs were structured.
Students who made predictions took longer to complete the lab than students who did not.
questions.explanation: Only choice B compares retention (quiz scores two weeks later) between students who predicted and those who did not. C, D, and A measure other things.

questions.passage: Archaeologists working at Çatalhöyük, a 9,000-year-old settlement in Turkey, have argued that its residents were unusually egalitarian, pointing to the absence of larger houses, public buildings, or streets that might mark a ruling class. Critics counter that inequality can exist without leaving such architectural traces.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the critics' position?
choices: Some burials beneath house floors contained far more obsidian tools and ornaments than others, though the houses themselves were of similar size.
Residents entered their houses through openings in the roof rather than doors.
Houses at Çatalhöyük were rebuilt on the same foundations for many generations.
The settlement's population grew steadily over several centuries.
questions.explanation: The critics claim inequality need not show up in architecture. Choice A shows unequal wealth in burials despite similar houses, exactly that pattern. C, D, and B say nothing about inequality.

questions.passage: Wildlife biologist Nadia Okonkwo and colleagues studied urban coyotes in Chicago and proposed that the animals have shifted to a mostly nocturnal schedule in order to avoid encounters with people.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' proposal?
choices: GPS collars showed that city coyotes were active mainly between midnight and 5 a.m., whereas rural coyotes in the same study were active at dawn and dusk.
Chicago's coyote population has increased over the past two decades.
Coyotes in city parks were most active in the hours when the parks were busiest with visitors.
Coyotes in Chicago eat a higher proportion of human food waste than coyotes in rural areas.
questions.explanation: The proposal has two parts: city coyotes are nocturnal, and this differs from what they would otherwise do. Choice A shows both, with a rural comparison group. Choice C suggests the opposite; D and B address other questions.

questions.passage: In her study of nineteenth-century sewing manuals, historian Clara Vance argues that the manuals were addressed not only to home seamstresses but also to women who hoped to earn money through dressmaking, and that publishers deliberately avoided saying so in order to preserve the manuals' respectable, domestic image.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Vance's argument?
choices: Advertisements for sewing manuals frequently appeared alongside advertisements for sewing machines.
Most sewing manuals of the period were published in cities where professional dressmaking was common.
Several manuals include detailed instructions for pricing garments and keeping accounts of customers' orders, while their prefaces describe the books as guides for 'the home.'
Sewing manuals were among the best-selling instructional books of the period.
questions.explanation: Vance's claim has two parts: the books served aspiring professionals, and the publishers hid that. Choice C supplies evidence of both: commercial content inside, domestic framing outside. The other findings are consistent with either view.

questions.passage:
Number of Public Libraries and Annual Visits in Four Towns, 2023

Town        Libraries  Annual visits
Brayford    2          84,000
Castleton   1          61,000
Dunmore     3          95,000
Ellery      2          38,000

A student notes that the town with the most libraries also had the most visits, but that the relationship between the number of libraries and the number of visits is not consistent across towns. For example, ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Castleton, with only 1 library, had more visits than Ellery, which has 2.
Ellery had the fewest visits of the four towns.
Brayford and Ellery each have 2 libraries.
Dunmore, with 3 libraries, had 95,000 visits.
questions.explanation: The claim is that the relationship is inconsistent. Choice A gives a case where a town with fewer libraries had more visits, which is the exception the student has in mind. D supports the first observation, not the second; C and B omit the comparison.

questions.passage:
Average Commute Time and Share of Workers Using Public Transit, Selected Cities, 2022

City         Avg. commute (min)  Transit share
Alder        34                  31%
Briar        22                  6%
Cedar        41                  55%
Downing      27                  12%

A transportation analyst claims that in these cities, higher use of public transit is associated with longer average commutes. She supports the claim by noting that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Downing has a transit share of 12%.
Cedar's transit share of 55% is more than nine times Briar's.
Briar has both the shortest average commute and the lowest transit share, while Cedar has the longest commute and the highest transit share.
Alder's average commute of 34 minutes is longer than Downing's 27 minutes.
questions.explanation: The claim is about an association between two variables, so the supporting data must pair them. Choice C does so at both extremes. D mentions only commutes; B only transit share; A is a single number.

questions.passage:
Results of a Trial Comparing Two Reading Interventions

Group          Students  Pretest mean  Posttest mean
Intervention A 120       41.2          58.7
Intervention B 118       40.9          52.3
Control        121       41.5          47.0

Researchers compared two reading interventions with a control group that received regular instruction. They concluded that Intervention A was the more effective of the two, noting that although ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
choices: Intervention A's posttest mean of 58.7 was the highest of the three groups, its pretest mean was the lowest.
Intervention B's group had the fewest students, its posttest mean exceeded that of the control group.
all three groups began with similar pretest means, Intervention A's group improved by about 17.5 points compared with about 11.4 for Intervention B and 5.5 for the control group.
the control group improved by 5.5 points, its pretest mean was the highest of the three.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is about relative effectiveness, so the relevant comparison is gain from pretest to posttest, after noting the groups started alike. Choice C does exactly that. A misstates the data (41.2 is not the lowest pretest); B and D compare the wrong things.

questions.passage: "The Poet," an 1844 essay by Ralph Waldo Emerson, argues that poetry is not a matter of ornament or meter but of insight: a true poet sees connections that others miss and finds the words for them.
questions.stem: Which quotation from "The Poet" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "For it is not metres, but a metre-making argument, that makes a poem."
"The poet is the sayer, the namer, and represents beauty."
"The poets are thus liberating gods."
"Language is fossil poetry."
questions.explanation: The claim contrasts meter and ornament with insight ('argument'). Choice A states precisely that a poem is made by its 'metre-making argument,' not by meter. The other quotations are about the poet's role or language, not this contrast.

questions.passage: Emily Dickinson's poems often treat abstract ideas as if they were physical objects or living creatures, giving intangible experiences a concrete, almost domestic presence.
questions.stem: Which quotation from a Dickinson poem most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "I heard a Fly buzz—when I died—"
"Because I could not stop for Death— / He kindly stopped for me—"
"I'm Nobody! Who are you? / Are you—Nobody—too?"
"There's a certain Slant of light, / Winter Afternoons—"
questions.explanation: Choice B personifies Death as a courteous driver who 'stopped for me,' turning an abstraction into a figure with manners. C addresses the reader, D describes light, and A reports a physical fly; none makes an abstraction concrete.

questions.passage: Sociologist Marcus Bell contends that the rise of online reviews has not, as is often claimed, given consumers more accurate information about restaurants, because reviewers disproportionately write after unusually good or unusually bad experiences.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Bell's contention?
choices: Online reviews of restaurants are on average longer than online reviews of other businesses.
Restaurants with more online reviews tend to have higher average ratings.
In a survey, most diners said they consult online reviews before choosing a restaurant.
When researchers surveyed a random sample of a restaurant's customers, the distribution of their satisfaction closely matched the distribution of ratings the restaurant had received online.
questions.explanation: Bell's claim is that online ratings misrepresent typical experiences. Choice D shows the ratings match a random sample of actual customers, which undercuts the claim directly. B, C, and A do not address accuracy.

questions.passage: Botanist Lena Marsh hypothesizes that the bright red color of a certain wildflower's petals serves to attract hummingbirds, which are its main pollinators.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?
choices: The wildflower blooms earlier in the spring than most other plants in its habitat.
Hummingbirds were observed feeding on several other plant species in the area.
Hummingbirds visited red-petaled plants far more often than plants of the same species whose petals had been painted white.
The wildflower's red pigment is chemically similar to that found in some fruits.
questions.explanation: Choice C isolates color: same species, same conditions, different petal color, different hummingbird visitation. The other findings do not connect color to hummingbird behavior.

questions.passage:
Estimated Population of Three Bird Species on an Island Before and After Rat Eradication

Species         2010 (before)  2020 (after)
Storm petrel    1,400          6,100
Shearwater      2,200          2,600
Tern            900            850

Conservationists removed invasive rats from the island in 2011, expecting seabird populations to recover. The results were uneven: ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: the shearwater population grew by 400 birds between 2010 and 2020.
the storm petrel population more than quadrupled, while the tern population was essentially unchanged.
all three species had larger populations in 2020 than in 2010.
the storm petrel population rose from 1,400 to 6,100.
questions.explanation: 'Uneven' calls for a contrast between species. Choice B pairs the largest gain with the species that did not recover. D and A each describe one species; C is false for the tern.

questions.passage: Literary scholar Priya Raman argues that the narrator of Charlotte Brontë's 1847 novel Jane Eyre repeatedly addresses the reader directly in order to enlist the reader as a witness to events that other characters refuse to acknowledge.
questions.stem: Which quotation from Jane Eyre most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?"
"Reader, I married him."
"I would always rather be happy than dignified."
"I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will."
questions.explanation: Only choice B addresses the reader directly. D and A are spoken to Rochester, and C is a general reflection; whatever their interest, they cannot illustrate a claim about direct address.

questions.passage: A city council member argues that a new protected bike lane on Main Street has made the street safer for everyone, not just cyclists.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the council member's argument?
choices: In the year after the lane was built, collisions involving pedestrians and cars on Main Street fell by 30 percent, and collisions involving cyclists fell by 45 percent.
Business owners on Main Street reported an increase in customers after the lane was built.
The number of cyclists using Main Street doubled in the year after the lane was built.
Most residents surveyed said they supported building more bike lanes.
questions.explanation: The argument is about safety 'for everyone,' so evidence must include non-cyclists. Choice A reports fewer pedestrian collisions as well as fewer cyclist collisions. C shows use, not safety; B and D are about business and opinion.

questions.passage: Vanilla is the second most expensive spice in the world after saffron. The vanilla orchid is pollinated naturally by a single species of bee found only in Mexico, so growers elsewhere must pollinate each flower by hand, on the one day it opens. Since a vanilla vine may produce hundreds of flowers, this means that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: growers outside Mexico must devote a great deal of labor to producing vanilla.
vanilla grown in Mexico is of higher quality than vanilla grown elsewhere.
the vanilla orchid is at risk of extinction outside Mexico.
saffron is also pollinated by hand.
questions.explanation: Hand-pollinating hundreds of flowers, each on its one open day, is enormously labor-intensive, which also fits the opening point about expense. B, C, and D introduce claims the text does not support.

questions.passage: The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze device recovered from a Greek shipwreck and dated to roughly 100 BCE, used dozens of interlocking gears to predict eclipses and the positions of the planets. Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity survives from the following thousand years; the next devices of similar sophistication are the astronomical clocks of the fourteenth century. Historians of technology therefore caution that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the mechanism was probably built much later than the shipwreck suggests.
fourteenth-century clockmakers must have studied the Antikythera mechanism.
ancient Greek astronomers were more accurate than their medieval successors.
the absence of surviving artifacts does not prove that a technology was absent.
questions.explanation: The point is that a sophisticated device existed yet nothing comparable survives for a millennium; the lesson is that gaps in the record need not mean gaps in the technology. A contradicts the dating; B and C are unsupported.

questions.passage:
The following text is from an 1899 novel. Miss Thorne is a schoolteacher in a small town.

Miss Thorne had lived in the village for eleven years, and in that time she had learned exactly which of her opinions could be spoken aloud at the general store and which were better kept for her letters to her sister in Boston. She had never once confused the two. And so when she heard herself say to Mr. Halloway, in front of three customers, that the new school board had 'the collective wisdom of a fence post,' she was ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: reminded of her sister's advice about the school board.
certain that Mr. Halloway would agree with her.
as astonished as anyone in the store.
pleased that her wit had finally found an audience.
questions.explanation: Miss Thorne has spent eleven years carefully separating public and private opinions and has 'never once confused the two.' Hearing herself blurt out a private opinion in public would therefore surprise her. The other completions ignore that setup.

questions.passage: Economists who study lotteries have noted a puzzle: ticket sales rise sharply as jackpots grow, even though the expected value of a ticket, the prize multiplied by the chance of winning, remains far below its price. Buyers do not appear to be miscalculating the odds; surveys show most know the odds are very poor. One proposed explanation is that a ticket is bought less as an investment than as a license to imagine a different life, and that this experience is worth more when the imagined life is more extravagant. If this explanation is correct, then ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: lottery tickets should be priced according to their expected value.
people who buy tickets should be less able than others to estimate probabilities.
lottery sales should fall when buyers are informed of the exact odds.
a larger jackpot should increase sales even when the odds of winning are made proportionally worse.
questions.explanation: If the value lies in imagining a more extravagant life, what matters is the jackpot's size, not the odds. Choice D follows. C and B assume buyers misjudge odds, which the text rules out; A is a recommendation the text does not support.

questions.passage: Cast iron pans are prized for holding heat, but they are also slow to heat up and have hot spots where the burner touches the pan. Professional cooks compensate by preheating cast iron for several minutes and by turning the pan during cooking. Home cooks who skip these steps often conclude that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the pan cooks unevenly, when the real problem is how it was used.
professional cooks prefer lighter pans.
cast iron is unsuitable for cooking on a gas burner.
cast iron pans hold heat better than other pans.
questions.explanation: Without preheating and turning, the pan's hot spots produce uneven results; a cook who skips those steps would blame the pan. The other conclusions do not follow from skipping the steps.

questions.passage: Recordings of humpback whale songs show that all the males in a population sing the same song in a given year, and that the song changes gradually over time. Occasionally, however, a population's song is replaced entirely within a season by the song of a neighboring population to the west. Because such wholesale replacement has been observed to travel only eastward across the South Pacific, researchers suspect that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the songs serve no function in attracting mates.
whale populations in the eastern Pacific are unable to produce new songs.
humpback whales in the Atlantic sing the same songs as those in the Pacific.
songs spread when a few whales from a western population migrate east and are imitated.
questions.explanation: Replacement always comes from the west and moves east, which suggests a directional carrier; a few migrating whales being imitated fits. B overreaches (songs also change gradually everywhere); A and C are unrelated.

questions.passage: Medieval European maps often placed Jerusalem at the center and east at the top. Modern viewers tend to treat this as evidence that the mapmakers were ignorant of geography. Yet the same mapmakers produced accurate coastal charts for sailors, with north at the top and no religious center. Historians who have compared the two kinds of maps conclude that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the symbolic maps reflect a choice about what a map was for, not a lack of knowledge.
the coastal charts were copied from ancient Roman sources.
medieval mapmakers gradually abandoned religious symbolism as their knowledge improved.
medieval sailors were more educated than medieval scholars.
questions.explanation: The same people made both accurate charts and symbolic maps, so the symbolic layout was a choice about purpose. D and B are unsupported; C implies a progression the text does not describe (the two coexisted).

questions.passage: The poet William Carlos Williams worked as a physician for over forty years, often writing poems on prescription pads between patients. He said that medicine gave him access to the everyday speech and lives of ordinary people, which became the raw material of his poetry. For Williams, then, his two careers were ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: kept strictly separate.
in constant conflict, each taking time from the other.
complementary, with one feeding the other.
equally unsatisfying.
questions.explanation: Medicine supplied the 'raw material' of the poetry, so the careers nourished each other. Choice B might be a common assumption but is not what the text says; A and D contradict it.

questions.passage: In an experiment, participants were asked to estimate how many jelly beans were in a jar. Individual guesses ranged widely, but the average of all guesses came within 3 percent of the true number. When the experiment was repeated with participants allowed to discuss their guesses before answering, the guesses clustered more tightly together, and the average was much less accurate. The researchers concluded that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: people are poor at estimating quantities.
the true number of jelly beans should have been revealed before the guessing.
the accuracy of a group's average depends on its members' errors being independent of one another.
discussion improves the accuracy of individual guesses.
questions.explanation: Without discussion, errors scattered in different directions and canceled out; discussion made the errors correlated and the average worse. That is the point of choice C. A ignores the accurate average; D is contradicted.

questions.passage: Linguists once believed that the world's languages divide sharply into those with tone, where pitch changes the meaning of a word, and those without. Recent surveys complicate the picture: many so-called non-tonal languages use pitch to distinguish a handful of word pairs, and many tonal languages have words whose tones are barely realized in fast speech. Some researchers now suggest that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the difference between tonal and non-tonal languages is one of degree rather than kind.
pitch plays no meaningful role in most languages.
tonal languages are gradually losing their tones.
tone is a feature of only a small number of the world's languages.
questions.explanation: Both categories show features of the other, so the line between them is blurry, a matter of degree. D and B contradict the surveys; C reads a trend into what is described as variation in fast speech.

questions.passage: Public health researchers found that after a city required chain restaurants to print calorie counts on menus, the average calories per order at those restaurants fell by about 4 percent. Orders at independent restaurants, which were exempt from the rule, did not change. However, the average calories per order at the chains had already fallen by 3 percent in the year before the rule took effect, as the chains reformulated their menus in anticipation. The researchers therefore argue that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: customers at chain restaurants are more health-conscious than customers elsewhere.
the calorie labels had no effect on what customers ordered.
independent restaurants should also be required to print calorie counts.
measuring the rule's effect only from the date it took effect understates its total impact.
questions.explanation: Part of the change happened before the rule's start date but because of the rule (chains changed menus in anticipation). Counting only from the start date would miss that part. B is contradicted; C and A are not argued.

questions.passage: Before the invention of the typewriter in the 1870s, business correspondence was written by clerks with excellent handwriting, and offices judged applicants largely on their penmanship. Within two decades, typing had become the standard, and handwriting ceased to matter for such jobs. This suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: handwriting is no longer taught in schools.
a skill can lose its value in the job market quickly when technology changes.
clerks in the 1870s were better educated than clerks today.
typewriters were expensive when they were first introduced.
questions.explanation: Penmanship went from decisive to irrelevant in twenty years because of a machine. Choice B states that general lesson. The others introduce claims the text does not make.

questions.passage: When the Voyager 1 spacecraft photographed Earth from six billion kilometers away in 1990, the planet occupied less than a single pixel. The image had almost no scientific value; the spacecraft's cameras were in fact switched off shortly afterward to save power. Yet the astronomer Carl Sagan had lobbied for years to take the picture, arguing that it would be worth more than any measurement. His reasoning suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: scientific instruments should be designed with photography in mind.
an image can have value in how it changes the way people see themselves, apart from any data it contains.
Sagan believed the cameras were more important than the other instruments.
the Voyager mission was primarily intended to photograph Earth.
questions.explanation: Sagan wanted a picture he knew had 'almost no scientific value,' so its worth must lie elsewhere, in its effect on people's perspective. A, D, and C misstate the mission or Sagan's priorities.

questions.passage: Farmers in some dry regions plant rows of trees as windbreaks around their fields. The trees compete with crops for water, so yields in the rows nearest the trees are lower than in the open. Nevertheless, most studies find that total yield across the whole field is higher with windbreaks than without them, which indicates that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the trees should be planted farther apart to reduce competition for water.
windbreaks are useful only in regions with heavy rainfall.
crops near windbreaks receive more sunlight than crops in the open.
the benefit of reduced wind across most of the field outweighs the loss near the trees.
questions.explanation: Yields drop next to the trees yet rise overall, so gains elsewhere in the field must exceed the local loss. A, C, and B are not supported by the comparison described.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a 1920 novel. Alma has returned to her family's house after several years abroad.

Everything was where it had been: the brass clock on the mantel, the chair with the worn arm, the smell of beeswax in the hall. Her mother had kept it all exactly so. Alma had expected to feel comforted. Instead she found that the sameness of the rooms made her own changes the more visible, as a still photograph makes plain how much its subject has moved. She understood then that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: she would need to rearrange the rooms before she could feel at home.
her mother had not wanted her to return.
her years abroad had been wasted.
the house, by staying the same, measured how much she herself had changed.
questions.explanation: The unchanged rooms act as a fixed reference, like a still photograph, against which Alma's own change becomes visible. B, A, and C add ideas the text does not contain.

questions.passage: Although the two warbler species look nearly identical, their songs are ______: experienced birders can tell them apart by ear from a hundred yards away.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: melodious
faint
seasonal
distinctive
questions.explanation: The birders can tell the species apart by their songs, so the songs must be distinctive. 'Faint' and 'melodious' describe volume and beauty, not difference; 'seasonal' is unrelated.

questions.passage: The museum's new wing was designed to be ______ with the original 1890s building: its brick facade, arched windows, and copper roof echo the older structure so closely that visitors often assume the two were built together.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: identical
contrasted
concealed
harmonious
questions.explanation: The new wing 'echoes' the old one, so it is harmonious with it. 'Contrasted' is the opposite; 'concealed' does not fit; 'identical' overstates it, since the text says visitors only 'assume' they were built together.

questions.passage: Historian Vera Lindqvist cautions that the diary of a nineteenth-century sea captain, though vivid, should not be treated as a ______ account of shipboard life: the captain wrote it for his family, and he plainly left out episodes that would have worried them.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: recent
comprehensive
lengthy
fictional
questions.explanation: The captain 'left out episodes,' so the diary is not comprehensive. It is not called fictional (it is vivid and true as far as it goes), and length and recency are not at issue.

questions.passage: The engineers' first prototype was ______: it worked only in dry weather, needed adjustment every few hours, and could not be operated by anyone but its designers. Still, it proved the idea could work.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: obsolete
temperamental
durable
efficient
questions.explanation: A device that fails in rain and needs constant adjustment is temperamental. 'Durable' and 'efficient' contradict the description; 'obsolete' means outdated, which a first prototype cannot be.

questions.passage: Some critics have called the novelist's late style ______, pointing to sentences that run for a page without a period; her admirers reply that the long sentences are carefully built and reward patient reading.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: undisciplined
sentimental
restrained
conventional
questions.explanation: Critics point to page-long sentences and admirers defend them as 'carefully built,' so the criticism must be that the style lacks discipline. 'Restrained' and 'conventional' are opposites of what is described; 'sentimental' concerns feeling, not sentence length.

questions.passage: The committee's report is ______ on the question of cost: it lists several possible funding sources but never says which the committee recommends or how much the project would require.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: adamant
equivocal
erroneous
exhaustive
questions.explanation: A report that lists options but avoids committing to any is equivocal. 'Exhaustive' would mean it covered the question thoroughly; 'adamant' means firm; 'erroneous' means wrong, which the text does not say.

questions.passage: Ecologists once regarded fire as purely destructive to forests, but many now consider periodic low-intensity burns to be ______ to the health of certain ecosystems, since they clear undergrowth and release seeds that require heat to germinate.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: incidental
subsequent
detrimental
integral
questions.explanation: The burns 'clear undergrowth and release seeds,' so they are integral, essential, to the ecosystem's health. 'Detrimental' is the old view the sentence contrasts with; 'incidental' means minor; 'subsequent' means following.

questions.passage: The recipe's instructions are ______: they specify the temperature of the water, the weight of the flour to the gram, and even the number of times the dough should be folded.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: vague
brief
precise
optional
questions.explanation: Temperature, weight to the gram, and number of folds are precise instructions. 'Vague' and 'brief' contradict the detail listed; 'optional' does not fit.

questions.passage: Because the archaeological site lies under a modern city, excavation has been ______: crews can dig only in the small plots that become available when old buildings are demolished, often waiting years between opportunities.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: piecemeal
expedited
controversial
unnecessary
questions.explanation: Digging 'only in small plots' with years between them is piecemeal work. 'Expedited' means sped up; 'unnecessary' and 'controversial' are not suggested.

questions.passage: The senator's speech was widely praised for its ______, but a close reading shows that its apparently plain statements were carefully hedged, leaving her room to reverse course later.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: brevity
eloquence
urgency
candor
questions.explanation: The 'but' signals that the praise was for a quality the speech only seemed to have; 'apparently plain statements' that were 'hedged' means it seemed candid but was not. Brevity, eloquence, and urgency are not contradicted by hedging.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from a 1913 travel memoir.

Our guide was a man of few words, and those few were ______; he would answer 'Perhaps' to a question about the weather and 'It has been known' to a question about bandits, so that we learned to read his face rather than his speech.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: noncommittal
reassuring
exaggerated
learned
questions.explanation: 'Perhaps' and 'It has been known' commit to nothing, so the guide's words are noncommittal. They are not reassuring (bandits!), not exaggerated, and there is no sign of learning.

questions.passage: Sea otters play a ______ role in kelp forests: by eating sea urchins, which would otherwise devour the kelp, they allow the forest to survive.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: crucial
mysterious
minor
temporary
questions.explanation: Without otters the kelp would be devoured, so their role is crucial. 'Minor' is the opposite; 'temporary' and 'mysterious' are not supported.

questions.passage: The philosopher's prose is famously ______; a single paragraph may take a reader an hour, not because the ideas are obscure but because every clause depends on a distinction made three pages earlier.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: polemical
dense
ornamental
accessible
questions.explanation: Prose in which every clause depends on earlier distinctions is dense. 'Accessible' is the opposite; 'polemical' means argumentative, and 'ornamental' means decorative, neither of which the description supports.

questions.passage: The town council's decision to close the library on Sundays was ______ by residents who pointed out that Sunday was the only day many working families could visit.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: anticipated
ratified
contested
overlooked
questions.explanation: Residents who 'pointed out' a problem with the decision were contesting it. 'Ratified' means approved; 'anticipated' and 'overlooked' do not fit the residents' objection.

questions.passage: Once considered a weed, purslane has recently been ______ by chefs, who prize its lemony flavor and crisp texture.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: embraced
cultivated
studied
dismissed
questions.explanation: The contrast with 'once considered a weed' and the chefs 'prizing' it points to 'embraced.' 'Dismissed' is the opposite; 'cultivated' and 'studied' are possible activities but do not capture the change in regard.

questions.passage: Far from being ______, the treaty's vague wording was deliberate: negotiators on both sides needed an agreement their governments could each interpret favorably at home.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: a triumph
intentional
a lapse
a compromise
questions.explanation: 'Far from being X, the wording was deliberate' requires X to mean the opposite of deliberate: a lapse, an oversight. 'Intentional' is a synonym of deliberate; 'compromise' and 'triumph' do not contrast with 'deliberate.'

questions.passage: Most people picture a desert as a sea of sand, but sand covers only about a fifth of the world's deserts. The rest is rock, gravel, salt flat, or, in the case of Antarctica, the largest desert of all, ice. What makes a place a desert is not what covers the ground but how little rain falls on it.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that Antarctica should not be classified as a desert.
To explain why so little rain falls in desert regions.
To correct a common misconception about what defines a desert.
To describe the plants and animals that live in deserts.
questions.explanation: The text opens with what 'most people picture,' gives contrary facts, and ends with the true definition. It does not describe wildlife, argue against Antarctica's status, or explain rainfall.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a 1905 novel.

It was Mr. Ashby's habit to read the newspaper at breakfast, and to read it aloud, and to pause after each item so that his family might admire the sagacity of his comments upon it. His daughters had long ago learned to say 'Indeed' at the right intervals without lifting their eyes from their plates. His wife, who had never learned this, was obliged each morning to hear the news twice: once from the paper and once from Mr. Ashby.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence?
choices: It reveals that Mr. Ashby is unaware of his family's feelings.
It suggests that Mrs. Ashby is more interested in the news than her daughters are.
It contrasts the wife's situation with the daughters' to emphasize how tiresome Mr. Ashby's habit is.
It explains why the family reads the newspaper at breakfast.
questions.explanation: The daughters have a way of ignoring the ritual; the wife has not, and so must endure it fully. The contrast underlines the tedium. B misreads 'obliged'; A may be true but is not what the sentence does; D is not addressed.

questions.passage: For decades, physicians told patients with lower back pain to rest in bed. Randomized trials in the 1990s found that patients who stayed active recovered faster and were less likely to develop chronic pain than those who rested. Guidelines have since reversed: bed rest is now discouraged for most back pain. The episode is often cited by advocates of evidence-based medicine as an example of how a plausible-sounding treatment can persist for years without ever being tested.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It explains the causes of back pain and then evaluates several remedies.
It presents two competing treatments and argues that one is superior.
It summarizes a debate among physicians and then proposes a compromise.
It describes a treatment, presents evidence that overturned it, and notes the broader lesson drawn from the reversal.
questions.explanation: The sequence is: old advice, trial evidence against it, changed guidelines, and the lesson advocates draw. There is no competition between remedies (B), no discussion of causes (A), and no compromise (C).

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Nathaniel Hawthorne's 1850 novel The Scarlet Letter.

The founders of a new colony, whatever Utopia of human virtue and happiness they might originally project, have invariably recognized it among their earliest practical necessities to allot a portion of the virgin soil as a cemetery, and another portion as the site of a prison.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the phrase 'whatever Utopia of human virtue and happiness they might originally project' in the text as a whole?
choices: It praises the idealism of the colony's founders.
It sets up an ironic contrast between the founders' hopes and the grim provisions they must make.
It suggests that the founders' plans for the colony were never carried out.
It explains why the founders chose the site for their colony.
questions.explanation: The sentence pits the founders' 'Utopia' against the 'practical necessities' of a cemetery and a prison, with 'whatever' and 'invariably' underscoring the irony. It neither praises the founders, explains the site, nor says the plans failed.

questions.passage: Baseball's 'seventh-inning stretch,' the custom of standing up midway through the seventh inning, is often credited to President William Howard Taft, who supposedly stood to stretch during a 1910 game and prompted the crowd to rise with him. The story is appealing but almost certainly false: newspaper accounts of fans standing to stretch in the seventh inning appear as early as 1869, forty years before Taft's game.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why the seventh inning was chosen for the stretch.
To cast doubt on a popular story about the origin of a custom.
To argue that President Taft was an important figure in baseball history.
To describe the origins of baseball's most important traditions.
questions.explanation: The text presents the Taft story and then gives evidence that the custom predates it. It does not survey traditions (D), explain the choice of inning (A), or praise Taft (C).

questions.passage: Photographs of Yosemite Valley taken in the 1860s show open meadows and widely spaced oaks. The same views today are dense with conifers. The change is often attributed to the suppression of natural fires, but historians add another cause: the Ahwahneechee people who lived in the valley had for centuries set deliberate burns to keep the meadows open, a practice that ended when they were forced from the valley in the 1850s.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence?
choices: It introduces the historians' explanation for the change.
It offers evidence that the photographs from the 1860s are inaccurate.
It establishes the change that the rest of the text sets out to explain.
It argues that conifers are better suited to the valley than oaks.
questions.explanation: Sentence one describes the past, sentence two the present; together they define the change ('The change is often attributed...') that the remaining sentences explain. B and D are not supported; A describes the last sentence.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Mary Shelley's 1818 novel Frankenstein. Victor Frankenstein describes his early studies.

Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate; I desire, therefore, in this narration, to state those facts which led to my predilection for that science. When I was thirteen years of age we all went on a party of pleasure to the baths near Thonon; the inclemency of the weather obliged us to remain a day confined to the inn. In this house I chanced to find a volume of the works of Cornelius Agrippa.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence?
choices: It describes the weather that trapped the narrator's family at the inn.
It introduces Cornelius Agrippa as the narrator's teacher.
It states the narrator's purpose in recounting the episode that follows.
It expresses the narrator's regret at having taken up science.
questions.explanation: The narrator announces what he intends to do: 'state those facts which led to my predilection for that science.' The anecdote then follows. A and B belong to later sentences; D reads in a feeling the sentence does not state.

questions.passage: A chess grandmaster shown a board position from a real game for five seconds can typically reproduce it almost perfectly, while a novice recalls only a few pieces. Shown a board with pieces placed at random, however, the grandmaster does little better than the novice. Psychologists take this as evidence that expert memory is not larger in general but organized around meaningful patterns, which random positions lack.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a common belief about expertise and presents evidence against it.
It compares two groups of players and concludes that one has a better memory.
It states a hypothesis and then describes an experiment designed to disprove it.
It reports a finding, then a second finding that qualifies the first, and then the interpretation the two together support.
questions.explanation: Finding one (experts excel on real positions), finding two (not on random ones), and the interpretation that reconciles them. B is wrong because the conclusion is that the memory is not larger in general; C and A do not match the sequence.

questions.passage: Want to keep cut flowers fresh longer? Trim the stems at an angle so they can take up more water, remove any leaves that would sit below the waterline, and change the water every two days. A teaspoon of sugar feeds the flowers; a few drops of bleach keeps bacteria from clogging the stems.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To give practical advice for extending the life of cut flowers.
To argue that fresh flowers are worth their cost.
To compare different varieties of flowers.
To explain why cut flowers wilt.
questions.explanation: The text is a list of instructions ('Trim,' 'remove,' 'change') with brief reasons. It does not explain wilting in general, compare varieties, or make a case about cost.

questions.passage: Some scholars of Beethoven's late string quartets describe them as the work of a composer who, having gone deaf, retreated into private abstraction. Yet the quartets were written on commission, rehearsed with the composer present, and revised after performances; Beethoven fought with his publisher over every detail of their printing. The image of the isolated genius, however romantic, does not survive contact with the documents.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence?
choices: It concedes that the scholars' description is partly accurate.
It provides examples of the abstraction that characterizes the late quartets.
It presents evidence that undermines the view described in the first sentence.
It explains why Beethoven's deafness affected his working methods.
questions.explanation: The first sentence gives a view (retreat into private abstraction); the second lists facts (commission, rehearsal, revision, disputes) that show engagement with the world; the third draws the conclusion. The sentence does not illustrate abstraction, explain deafness, or concede anything.

questions.passage:
The following text is from an 1891 short story.

The letter had been on the hall table for three days. Each morning Mrs. Garrow picked it up, turned it over to look at the seal, and set it down again, a little farther from the edge than before, as if it might otherwise fall and open itself.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the detail that the letter is set down 'a little farther from the edge than before'?
choices: It suggests that the hall table is too small for its purpose.
It conveys Mrs. Garrow's reluctance to confront the letter's contents while hinting that she cannot quite leave it alone.
It shows that Mrs. Garrow is careless with her correspondence.
It indicates that the letter has already been opened.
questions.explanation: She handles the letter daily but pushes it away each time, 'as if it might otherwise fall and open itself,' so she is both drawn to it and avoiding it. C is contradicted by her care; A and D are not supported.

questions.passage: In the 1850s the physician John Snow mapped the homes of London cholera victims and found them clustered around a single public water pump on Broad Street. When the pump's handle was removed, new cases in the area fell sharply. Snow's map is now taught as a founding example of epidemiology, but at the time it convinced few of his colleagues, who continued to blame the disease on bad air.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that Snow's colleagues were incompetent.
To describe how public water pumps were built in Victorian London.
To recount an early epidemiological investigation and note how it was received in its time.
To explain how cholera is transmitted.
questions.explanation: The text narrates Snow's investigation and ends with its lukewarm contemporary reception. It is not about the biology of cholera, does not attack colleagues, and says nothing about pump construction.

questions.passage: Translators of poetry face a choice that has no right answer. Preserve the meter and rhyme, and the meaning bends to fit them; preserve the meaning, and the poem arrives as prose. Vladimir Nabokov, translating Pushkin, chose meaning so uncompromisingly that his version came with a commentary longer than the poem. His critics called the result unreadable. He called their alternative a lie.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final two sentences?
choices: They argue that Nabokov's approach to translation was the correct one.
They illustrate, through one translator's case, the irreconcilable positions described in the opening sentence.
They resolve the dilemma presented at the beginning of the text.
They explain why Pushkin's poetry is difficult to translate.
questions.explanation: The critics' verdict ('unreadable') and Nabokov's reply ('a lie') dramatize the two sides of the 'choice that has no right answer.' The text does not resolve the dilemma, take Nabokov's side, or discuss Pushkin specifically.

questions.passage: Honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs, sealed for three thousand years, has been reported to be still edible. Honey resists spoilage because it is mostly sugar with very little water, an environment in which bacteria cannot grow, and because bees add an enzyme that produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a natural preservative.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes an experiment and then reports its results.
It makes a claim and then acknowledges evidence against it.
It compares honey with other foods and ranks them by shelf life.
It presents a surprising fact and then explains the reasons behind it.
questions.explanation: The surprising fact (edible after three thousand years) is followed by two reasons (low water content; hydrogen peroxide). There is no experiment, no counterevidence, and no comparison.

questions.passage:
Text 1
The four-day workweek, in which employees work about 32 hours for the same pay, has been tried by dozens of companies. Advocates argue that rested workers are more productive, and several trials have reported that output held steady or rose after the change.

Text 2
Most published trials of the four-day week involve companies that volunteered to participate, often after their leaders had already decided the idea was promising. Such firms are not typical, and their results may not transfer to workplaces where the change is imposed rather than chosen.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the advocates' argument described in Text 1?
choices: By claiming that the trials were too short to show any effect.
By arguing that productivity is the wrong measure of a workplace policy.
By pointing out that the companies in the trials may not represent workplaces in general.

In addition,
Even so,
questions.explanation: Praise followed by refusal is a contrast that 'even so' expresses ('despite that'). 'Accordingly' and 'to that end' would make the refusal follow from the praise; 'in addition' treats them as parallel.

questions.passage: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995. Within a decade, elk herds that had grazed the river valleys unchecked became warier and moved to higher ground; willows and aspens along the rivers, ______ began to recover.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: by contrast,
in turn,
at any rate,
for that matter,
questions.explanation: The willows recovered as a further consequence of the elk moving away, a chain of effects that 'in turn' marks. 'By contrast' implies opposition; the other two are asides.

questions.passage: Many fruits are picked before they are ripe so that they survive shipping. Bananas, ______ are harvested green and ripened with ethylene gas after they reach their destination.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: as a result,
in short,
on the other hand,
for instance,
questions.explanation: Bananas are an example of the general practice just described; 'for instance' introduces it. 'On the other hand' would signal an exception, which bananas are not.

questions.passage: The study found that participants who slept fewer than six hours performed worse on memory tests than those who slept eight. The effect was not large; ______ it was consistent across every age group tested, which the researchers found more striking than its size.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: in fact,
as a result,
however,
on the contrary,
questions.explanation: 'Not large' is followed by a redeeming quality, 'consistent,' so a concessive contrast is needed: 'however.' 'On the contrary' would deny the smallness; 'in fact' would intensify it; 'as a result' makes no sense.

questions.passage: Lighthouses once required a keeper to live on site, trim the wicks, and wind the clockwork that turned the lens. ______ nearly all lighthouses are automated, and the keeper's cottages have become museums or rentals.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Otherwise,
Today,
Granted,
Indeed,
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the past ('once') to the present; 'today' marks that shift. 'Otherwise' and 'granted' imply conditions or concessions not present; 'indeed' would intensify the previous point rather than change time.

questions.passage: To make paper by hand, a papermaker first beats plant fibers into a pulp and suspends them in water. ______ she dips a screen into the vat and lifts it out, leaving a thin mat of fibers on the mesh.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Regardless,
In contrast,
However,
Next,
questions.explanation: The text gives steps in order ('first...'), so the following step takes 'next.' The other transitions signal contrast or dismissal, which have no place in a sequence of steps.

questions.passage: Critics of the new stadium argued that public money should not subsidize a private team. Supporters countered that the stadium would create jobs and draw visitors downtown. ______ both sides agreed that the traffic plan for game days was inadequate.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Therefore,
Nonetheless,
For example,
Similarly,
questions.explanation: After a disagreement, the sentence reports a point of agreement: a contrast with the dispute, which 'nonetheless' captures. 'Therefore' and 'similarly' do not fit the reversal, and the agreement is not an example.

questions.passage: Hummingbirds have the highest metabolism of any vertebrate and must eat almost constantly while awake. At night, ______ they enter a state of torpor in which their body temperature and heart rate drop dramatically, allowing them to survive until morning without feeding.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: thus,
moreover,
namely,
though,
questions.explanation: Day (constant eating) versus night (torpor, no eating) is a contrast; 'though' marks it. 'Moreover' adds, 'namely' specifies, and 'thus' concludes, none of which fits.

questions.passage: The town's annual kite festival draws thousands of visitors. Local businesses ______ report their highest sales of the year during the festival weekend.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: nevertheless
accordingly
conversely
previously
questions.explanation: High sales follow from the crowds; 'accordingly' marks that consequence. 'Nevertheless' and 'conversely' signal contrast, and 'previously' signals an earlier time.

questions.passage: The manuscript's handwriting matches that of the poet's secretary, not the poet. This does not mean the poem is not hers; ______ she is known to have dictated much of her late work.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: subsequently,
after all,
in contrast,
otherwise,
questions.explanation: The clause after the blank gives the reason the handwriting is not evidence against her authorship; 'after all' introduces such a supporting reason. The other transitions signal contrast, sequence, or an alternative condition.

questions.passage: Spinach is often described as an exceptional source of iron. ______ it contains about the same amount as many other leafy greens; the reputation appears to stem from a decimal-point error in a nineteenth-century nutrition table.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Similarly,
For example,
Consequently,
In reality,
questions.explanation: A reputation is followed by the fact that contradicts it; 'in reality' introduces the correction. The other transitions would treat the second sentence as parallel, resulting, or illustrative.

questions.passage: The Sámi people of northern Scandinavia have herded reindeer for ______ today, about 10 percent of Sámi are still involved in herding.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: centuries;
centuries, and
centuries
centuries,
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses ('The Sámi... have herded reindeer for centuries' and 'today, about 10 percent... are still involved') need a semicolon or a period between them. A comma alone (D) is a comma splice, no punctuation (C) is a run-on, and 'and' after a comma (B) would leave 'today' awkwardly attached.

questions.passage: In 1932 the physicist James Chadwick discovered the ______ a particle with no electric charge that sits in the nucleus of every atom except ordinary hydrogen.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: neutron, it is
neutron;
neutron
neutron:
questions.explanation: What follows the blank is an appositive that defines the neutron, so a colon introduces it. A semicolon (B) requires an independent clause after it; 'neutron, it is' (A) creates a comma splice; no punctuation (C) runs the definition into the sentence.

questions.passage: Although the Great Wall of China is often said to be visible from ______ astronauts have consistently reported that it cannot be seen with the naked eye from orbit.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: space,
space;
space, and
space
questions.explanation: 'Although... space' is a dependent clause, so it is joined to the main clause with a comma. A semicolon (B) would require two independent clauses, and 'and' (C) would leave the 'although' clause without a main clause to modify.

questions.passage: The photographer Dorothea Lange, whose 1936 portrait Migrant Mother became an emblem of the Great ______ took the picture in about ten minutes at a pea-pickers' camp in California.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Depression;
Depression,
Depression, and
Depression
questions.explanation: The 'whose...' clause is a nonessential modifier set off by commas; the second comma must close it before the main verb 'took.' A semicolon (A) cannot appear inside a clause, and 'and' (C) would make 'took' part of the modifier and leave the sentence without a main verb.

questions.passage: Three instruments dominate the traditional music of the Andes: the charango, a small guitar-like instrument originally made from an armadillo ______ the quena, an end-blown flute; and the bombo, a large drum.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: shell
shell, and
shell;
shell,
