questions.explanation: The list items themselves contain commas, so they are separated by semicolons; the second item already ends with a semicolon, so the first must too. A comma (D) would make the boundaries of the items unclear.

questions.passage: Researchers who study sleep distinguish between two broad ______ rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most dreaming occurs, and non-REM sleep, which is divided into three stages of increasing depth.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: kinds
kinds:
kinds,
kinds;
questions.explanation: The two kinds are then named, so a colon introduces the list. A semicolon (D) needs an independent clause; a comma (C) or nothing (A) leaves the list unintroduced.

questions.passage: The first successful vaccine, developed by Edward Jenner in ______ used material from cowpox lesions to protect against smallpox, a far deadlier disease.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: 1796, which
questions.explanation: 'Developed by Edward Jenner in 1796' is a nonessential participial phrase that began after the comma following 'vaccine'; it must close with a comma before the main verb 'used.' Adding 'which' (B) would turn 'used' into part of a relative clause and leave the sentence without a main verb.

questions.passage: Maria Tallchief was the first Native American to become a prima ballerina at a major ______ she danced with the New York City Ballet from 1947 to 1965.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: company
company;
company,
company and
questions.explanation: Both parts are complete sentences, so they must be joined by a semicolon (or separated by a period). A comma alone creates a comma splice; 'and' without a comma (D) joins independent clauses improperly.

questions.passage: Because a violin's sound depends on the exact thickness of its wooden ______ makers carve each plate by hand, tapping it and listening to the pitch as they go.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: plates,
plates;
plates, so
plates
questions.explanation: The 'Because...' clause is dependent and takes a comma before the main clause. 'So' (C) is redundant with 'because' and incorrect; a semicolon (B) needs independent clauses on both sides.

questions.passage: The Rosetta Stone, discovered by French soldiers in 1799, carries the same decree in three ______ hieroglyphic Egyptian, Demotic Egyptian, and ancient Greek, and it was the Greek that allowed scholars to begin deciphering the other two.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: scripts;
scripts:
scripts,
scripts
questions.explanation: The three scripts are listed after the blank, so a colon introduces them. A comma (C) would produce an ambiguous string of commas; a semicolon (A) requires an independent clause.

questions.passage: The word 'quarantine' comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, meaning 'forty ______ in the fourteenth century, ships arriving in Venice during plague outbreaks were required to anchor for forty days before landing.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: days'
days,'
days':
days';
questions.explanation: The quotation ends the first independent clause; a second independent clause follows ('ships... were required...'). A semicolon joins them. The closing quotation mark goes before the semicolon. A comma (B) creates a comma splice, and a colon (C) would present the second clause as an explanation of the first, which it is not exactly (it is a related historical fact).

questions.passage: The Grand Canyon is about 277 miles ______ at its widest point it spans 18 miles from rim to rim.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: long, and
long,
long and
long
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction ('and'). Without the comma (C) or the conjunction (B), the join is incorrect; with nothing (D) it is a run-on.

questions.passage: What makes the Antarctic icefish unusual is not its transparent blood, though that is striking ______ it is the fact that the fish has no hemoglobin at all, the only known vertebrate of which this is true.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: enough,
enough:
enough
enough;
questions.explanation: 'What makes... striking enough' is an independent clause; 'it is the fact...' is another. A semicolon separates them. A comma (A) splices them; a colon (B) would make the second clause an explanation of the first rather than the contrasting completion the 'not... it is' structure sets up.

questions.passage: Vera Rubin's measurements of galaxy rotation in the ______ showed that stars at a galaxy's edge move as fast as those near its center, a result that could be explained only by large amounts of unseen matter.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: 'Vera Rubin's measurements... in the 1970s' is the subject; 'showed' is its verb. No punctuation may separate a subject from its verb. Each of the other choices inserts a break in the wrong place.

questions.passage: The recipe calls for three ______ flour, butter, and a pinch of salt.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: ingredients;
ingredients,
ingredients
ingredients:
questions.explanation: A colon introduces the list that completes the sentence. A comma (B) would turn 'flour' into a fourth ingredient in a confusing series; a semicolon (A) requires a full clause after it.

questions.passage: Each of the museum's three Vermeer paintings ______ displayed in its own alcove, lit to reproduce the soft daylight of the artist's studio.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: are
is
have been
were
questions.explanation: The subject is 'each,' which is singular, so the verb is 'is.' The plural noun 'paintings' inside the prepositional phrase does not govern the verb.

questions.passage: After the storm passed, the volunteers spent the morning clearing branches from the road and ______ the fallen fence.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: repairing
they repaired
repaired
to repair
questions.explanation: The two activities are parallel objects of 'spent the morning': 'clearing... and repairing.' The other forms break the parallel structure.

questions.passage: By the time the expedition reached the summit, the climbers ______ for nineteen hours without rest.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: will have moved
have moved
had been moving
are moving
questions.explanation: 'By the time the expedition reached' places the action in the past before another past event, so the past perfect progressive 'had been moving' is required. The other tenses do not fit a completed past sequence.

questions.passage: Neither the director nor the producers ______ willing to comment on reports that the film's release would be delayed.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: is
has been
were
was
questions.explanation: With 'neither... nor,' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'producers,' which is plural: 'were.' The singular options agree with 'director,' which is farther from the verb.

questions.passage: Discovered in a Portuguese cave in 1998, ______ was the first strong evidence that Neanderthals and modern humans had interbred.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: a child's skeleton with a mixture of Neanderthal and modern human features
archaeologists identified a child's skeleton with a mixture of features, which
the skeleton of a child was found to mix Neanderthal and modern human features, and it
there was a child's skeleton with a mixture of features that
questions.explanation: The opening participial phrase 'Discovered in a Portuguese cave' must modify the thing discovered, which choice A places immediately after it. B makes 'archaeologists' the thing discovered (a dangling modifier); C and D also fail to put the skeleton directly after the modifier and add clumsy clauses.

questions.passage: The committee has recommended that the library ______ its hours on weekends to accommodate students who work during the week.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: extend
extending
extends
will extend
questions.explanation: After 'recommended that,' the verb takes the subjunctive form, 'extend' (the base form), regardless of the subject's number. 'Extends' and 'will extend' are indicative; 'extending' is not a finite verb.

questions.passage: The novel's reputation, which had declined steadily in the decades after its publication, ______ revived in the 1960s by a generation of critics who admired its formal experiments.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: being
having been
was
were
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular 'reputation' (the 'which' clause is a parenthetical modifier), and the sentence needs a main finite verb: 'was revived.' 'Were' does not agree, and 'having been' and 'being' leave the sentence without a main verb.

questions.passage: Ravens are among the few animals known to use gestures, such as pointing with ______ beaks to draw another raven's attention to an object.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: its
it's
their
there
questions.explanation: The possessive pronoun must refer to the plural 'ravens,' so 'their.' 'Its' is singular; 'it's' means 'it is'; 'there' is not a possessive.

questions.passage: The two proposals differ mainly in cost: the first would require new construction, ______ the second would adapt an existing building.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: whereas
as well as
moreover
consequently
questions.explanation: The two clauses contrast, and 'whereas' is a conjunction that joins them correctly. 'Consequently' and 'moreover' are adverbs that would produce a comma splice, and 'as well as' does not make sense between two clauses.

questions.passage: Unlike her contemporaries, who painted landscapes and street scenes, ______ concentrated on interiors and still lifes, rarely leaving her apartment to work.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Lise Brandt's canvases
the painter Lise Brandt
the paintings of Lise Brandt
it was the painter Lise Brandt who
questions.explanation: 'Unlike her contemporaries' compares people, and the main clause's actions ('concentrated,' 'leaving her apartment') belong to a person, so the subject must be 'the painter Lise Brandt.' A and C compare people to canvases or paintings, which cannot leave an apartment; D is ungrammatical after the opening phrase.

questions.passage: Bioluminescent plankton produce light when they are disturbed, ______ waves and boat wakes glow blue at night.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: which makes
making
they make
and making
questions.explanation: 'Which makes' correctly attaches a relative clause whose subject is the whole preceding fact. 'They make' creates a comma splice; 'making' would ambiguously modify 'plankton' or 'disturbed'; 'and making' has no subject.

questions.passage: Scientists estimate that the Amazon River discharges more water into the ocean than the next seven largest rivers ______
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: combined.
do combined.
have combined.
combined do.
questions.explanation: The comparison is 'more water than the next seven largest rivers combined,' where 'combined' modifies 'rivers.' Adding 'do' (D, B) is awkward and unnecessary, and 'have combined' (C) changes the meaning.

questions.passage: The astronomer's notebooks, along with the correspondence she kept with colleagues across Europe, ______ how quickly news of the comet's discovery spread.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: revealing
has revealed
reveal
reveals
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural 'notebooks'; the phrase 'along with the correspondence...' is a modifier and does not make the subject compound or singular. The verb is therefore 'reveal.' 'Revealing' is not a finite verb.

questions.passage: To reduce injuries, the league now requires that every player ______ a mouthguard and prohibits tackles above the shoulders.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: wear
is wearing
wore
wears
questions.explanation: After 'requires that,' the subjunctive base form 'wear' is used. The indicative forms in the other choices are incorrect in this construction.

questions.passage: The lighthouse keeper's daughter, Ida Lewis, ______ credited with saving at least eighteen people from drowning during her years at Lime Rock, Rhode Island.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: being
is
are
were
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular 'daughter' (Ida Lewis is an appositive), and the sentence needs a finite verb: 'is credited.' 'Being' leaves the sentence without a main verb.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Many gardeners hang nest boxes to help songbirds, and in some suburbs the boxes have clearly increased the number of birds nesting nearby. Nature writer Helen Ostrowski calls nest boxes one of the simplest and most effective ways for ordinary people to support bird populations.

Text 2
Ecologist Dev Raghunathan found that in areas where nest boxes were plentiful but insects were scarce, birds nested in large numbers yet raised fewer chicks per nest than birds in areas with fewer boxes and more insects. A nest box, he argues, can draw breeding birds to a place without providing what they need to raise their young.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Raghunathan (Text 2) most likely respond to Ostrowski's claim in Text 1?
choices: By cautioning that increasing the number of birds nesting in an area does not necessarily help bird populations if food is scarce.
By agreeing that nest boxes are the most effective way to support birds in every setting.
By arguing that songbirds rarely nest in boxes put up by gardeners.
By claiming that insects are more plentiful in suburbs than in other areas.
questions.explanation: Raghunathan grants that boxes attract nesting birds but shows that, where insects are scarce, those birds raise fewer young, so more nests need not mean healthier populations. Choice C contradicts his finding that birds nested 'in large numbers.'

questions.passage: Urban designer Adaeze Collins argues that how often a public plaza is used depends less on how attractive it looks than on whether it offers places to sit. In her view, plazas that are widely admired in photographs often go largely unused if they lack seating.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Collins's argument?
choices: Plazas with fountains attracted more visitors in summer than in winter.
In surveys, people rated plazas with plenty of seating as more attractive than plazas with little seating.
Among twelve plazas in one city, two that had won design awards but offered no benches drew the fewest visitors, while a plain plaza lined with movable chairs drew the most.
Plazas that had won design awards were photographed more often than plazas that had not.
questions.explanation: Collins claims that seating matters more than looks, and choice C sets admired but seatless plazas against a plain plaza with chairs and finds that the plain one draws more visitors. Choice B links seating to how attractive a plaza looks rather than to how much it is used, so it does not separate the two factors.

questions.passage: Before steel frames came into use, the height of a masonry building was limited by its walls. Because the walls had to carry the entire weight of the floors above them, a taller building needed thicker walls at its base, and those thick walls took up space that could otherwise have been used inside. Steel frames changed this by carrying the building's weight themselves, which allowed walls to be thin and buildings to rise much higher.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that masonry buildings are more durable than steel-framed buildings.
To describe the interiors of the first tall buildings.
To compare the costs of masonry and steel as building materials.
To explain how a structural innovation removed a limit on the height of buildings.
questions.explanation: The text sets out the limit that load-bearing walls placed on height and then shows how steel frames removed it. It makes no claim about durability (A) or cost (C).

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story.

Odile had run the bait shop at the end of the wharf for thirty years, and she was as ______ with praise as she was with credit. The fishermen could count on one hand the times she had called a catch a good one, and not one of them had ever walked out of her shop owing her money.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: lavish
sparing
candid
impulsive
questions.explanation: Odile rarely praises a catch and never lets anyone buy on credit, so she is sparing with both. 'Candid' might describe how she judges a catch, but it makes no sense with 'credit'; 'lavish' is the opposite.

questions.passage: Engineers designing buildings for earthquake-prone regions once aimed to make structures as rigid as possible, reasoning that a stiff building would resist shaking. Experience showed, however, that rigid buildings often cracked, because they could not absorb the energy of the ground's motion. Many modern designs therefore place flexible bearings between a building and its foundation, allowing the ground to shift beneath the building while the structure above moves much less. This approach suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: buildings in earthquake-prone regions should be built only on soft ground.
rigid buildings are no longer constructed anywhere in the world.
in earthquake design, allowing some movement can protect a building better than trying to resist all movement.
flexible bearings make buildings less expensive to construct.
questions.explanation: Rigid buildings cracked, while bearings that let the ground move beneath the building protect it, so permitting movement works better than resisting it. Choice B overstates the text, which describes a shift in 'many modern designs,' not the end of rigid buildings.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story. Emrys's father has fished from the same harbor all his life.

Emrys's father never spoke of the sea as beautiful. He spoke of it the way other men spoke of their employers: its moods, its unreasonable demands, the days it paid and the days it did not. Yet every morning, long before the boats went out, he stood at the kitchen window with his coffee and watched the water turn from black to gray to silver, and on the mornings Emrys joined him, neither of them said a word until the light was full.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although Emrys's father speaks of the sea only in practical terms, his daily habit suggests a deeper attachment to it.
Emrys's father resents the sea because it has made his livelihood unpredictable.
Emrys and his father rarely speak because they disagree about the fishing trade.
Emrys's father would rather watch the sea than fish on it.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts the father's businesslike talk about the sea ('Yet') with his silent daily ritual of watching it, which reveals feeling he does not express. Choice B takes the first half of that contrast for the whole; nothing in the text suggests resentment or disagreement.

questions.passage: When a predator approaches, the eastern hognose snake may flatten its neck, hiss loudly, and, if that ______ roll onto its back and lie still with its mouth hanging open.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: fails
fails;
fails:
fails,
questions.explanation: The clause 'if that fails' interrupts the list and is set off by a comma on each side; the first comma already appears after 'and,' so a second is needed after 'fails.' A semicolon or colon cannot separate the verb 'roll' from the rest of the series.

questions.passage: The owners of the small hardware store on Linden Avenue ______ offered free repair workshops for local residents every Saturday since the store first opened in 1998.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: has
have
having
was
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural 'owners,' so the verb is 'have offered.' 'Has' agrees with the singular 'store,' which is part of a prepositional phrase, and 'having' does not produce a complete sentence.

questions.passage: In many traditional Japanese houses, rooms are separated by sliding panels rather than by fixed walls. ______ a single large space can be divided into several smaller rooms at night and opened up again during the day.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Because of this,
Nevertheless,
By contrast,
Previously,
questions.explanation: Being able to divide and reopen a space follows from using sliding panels instead of fixed walls, so a cause-and-effect transition is needed. 'Nevertheless' and 'by contrast' signal a contrast that is not there, and 'previously' misplaces the sequence in time.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Entomologist Yusuf Adebayo studied a colony of harvester ants in a desert grassland.
• Each morning, a few 'patroller' ants left the nest before any of the foragers.
• When the patrollers returned safely, the foragers began leaving the nest to collect seeds.
• When the patrollers did not return, the foragers stayed inside.
• Adebayo concluded that patrollers help the colony judge whether conditions outside are safe.
questions.stem: The student wants to describe what the foragers did when the patrollers failed to return. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Each morning, a few patroller ants left the nest before any of the foragers.
Yusuf Adebayo studied a colony of harvester ants in a desert grassland.
When the patrollers did not return, the foragers stayed inside the nest.
When the patrollers returned safely, the foragers left the nest to collect seeds.
questions.explanation: The goal concerns the foragers' behavior when patrollers failed to return, which only choice C describes. Choice D describes the opposite case, when the patrollers came back.

questions.passage: Music historian Adaeze Montrose-Kiel finds early reviews of the player piano, a piano that plays itself from rolls of punched paper, strikingly ______: many critics praised the machine's flawless accuracy in one sentence and, in the next, complained that the same accuracy made its music sound lifeless, without ever acknowledging the tension between the two judgments.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: self-contradictory
effusive
perfunctory
prescient
questions.explanation: Critics who praise and condemn the same quality without noticing the conflict are self-contradictory. 'Effusive' (gushing with praise) fits only the first half of their reviews; 'perfunctory' (done with little care) and 'prescient' (showing foresight) do not describe the conflict the text emphasizes.

questions.passage: When lava erupts underwater, as it does along ridges on the ocean floor, cold seawater chills its outer surface almost instantly, forming a thin crust. Pressure from the molten rock inside soon breaks through the crust, and a new blob of lava squeezes out and is chilled in turn. Repeated many times, this process builds heaps of rounded, pillow-shaped lumps. Geologists who find such 'pillow lava' on dry land can therefore conclude that the rock there formed beneath water.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lava cools more slowly underwater than it does on land.
Most of the ocean floor is covered by pillow lava.
Pillow lava forms through a distinctive underwater process, so its presence reveals where rock once formed beneath water.
Geologists disagree about how pillow lava came to be found on dry land.
questions.explanation: The text explains how pillow lava forms underwater and why that makes it evidence of an underwater origin. Choice A contradicts the statement that seawater chills the lava 'almost instantly'; B and D are not discussed.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Music historian Rafael Duvenage-Oyelowo argues that sound recording, invented in the late nineteenth century, reduced musical variety. Once listeners could hear a celebrated performance again and again, he contends, local musicians began imitating it, and regional ways of playing the same tunes gradually disappeared.

Text 2
Recording also preserved regional styles that would otherwise have vanished. In the early twentieth century, folklorists carried portable recording machines into the countryside and captured fiddlers and singers whose ways of playing were already fading as younger people moved to cities. Many musicians today learn those older styles directly from the recordings.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Duvenage-Oyelowo's argument?
choices: By arguing that local musicians rarely imitated the celebrated performances they heard on recordings.
By noting that recording also helped preserve some of the regional styles that were disappearing.
By claiming that regional styles faded mainly because rural musicians could not afford recording machines.
By agreeing that recording has had only harmful effects on musical variety.
questions.explanation: Text 2 does not deny that recording affected regional styles; it adds that recording also 'preserved regional styles that would otherwise have vanished.' Choice A disputes a claim Text 2 never challenges, D ignores Text 2's point, and C is not supported.

questions.passage: A cluster of about a dozen craters lies on the Kessen Plain, the largest of them roughly 300 meters across. Many geologists have assumed that the craters formed at the same moment, when a single meteorite broke apart in the atmosphere and its fragments struck the ground together. Geologist Maren Achterberg-Osei argues instead that the craters record several separate impacts spread over thousands of years.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Achterberg-Osei's argument?
choices: The craters range widely in size, from a few meters to about 300 meters across.
Fragments of meteoritic iron recovered from the craters all share the same unusual chemical composition.
The craters are arranged in a narrow oval pattern that points in a single direction.
The oldest sediment layers filling the craters differ in age from crater to crater by several thousand years.
questions.explanation: If the craters formed at different times, the sediment that began filling each one should date from different times, which is what choice D describes. Choice A fits either account, since a meteorite that breaks apart makes fragments of many sizes; B and C point toward a single meteorite, the view Achterberg-Osei rejects.

questions.passage: When speakers of several different languages must communicate regularly, as in trade, they often develop a pidgin: a simplified language with a small vocabulary and few grammatical rules, used only in limited situations. No one speaks a pidgin as a first language. When children grow up hearing a pidgin as their main language, however, they tend to expand it, adding vocabulary and grammatical rules until it can express anything their parents' languages could. Linguists call the result a creole. It follows that a creole, unlike a pidgin, ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: has a smaller vocabulary than the languages from which it developed.
is used mainly for trade between speakers of different languages.
is the first language of at least some of its speakers.
has no grammatical rules of its own.
questions.explanation: A pidgin has no first-language speakers, but a creole arises when children grow up speaking it as their main language, so a creole has native speakers. Choice A contradicts the description of children expanding the language, B describes the pidgin's limited use, and D contradicts the added grammatical rules.

questions.passage: On a clear night, most stars look like tiny white points. A closer look, especially through binoculars, shows that stars actually come in a range of colors, from reddish orange to bluish white. These colors are not random: they reveal how hot each star's surface is. The coolest stars glow red, somewhat like the embers of a campfire, while the hottest shine a brilliant blue-white.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain what the colors of stars reveal about them.
To argue that binoculars are necessary for observing stars.
To describe how a star's color changes as it ages.
To compare the sizes of red stars and blue stars.
questions.explanation: The text notes that stars differ in color and then explains that color indicates surface temperature. Binoculars are mentioned only as one way to see the colors (B), and the text says nothing about aging (C) or size (D).

questions.passage: In some lakes that freeze over every winter, sediment settles in distinct bands called varves. Each varve consists of two layers deposited over the course of a single ______ a light, coarse layer laid down in summer, when streams carry sand and silt into the lake, and a dark, fine layer laid down in winter, when only clay drifts slowly to the bottom.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: year;
year
year, they are
year:
questions.explanation: What follows the blank is a list that spells out the 'two layers,' not an independent clause, so a colon introduces it. A semicolon (A) must join two independent clauses, no punctuation (B) runs the list into the sentence, and ', they are' (C) creates a comma splice.

questions.passage: Every Sunday afternoon, my grandmother and her three sisters ______ around the kitchen table to play cards, trade family news, and argue cheerfully about whose turn it is to deal.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: gathers
gather
is gathering
has gathered
questions.explanation: The subject, 'my grandmother and her three sisters,' is plural because its parts are joined by 'and,' so it takes the plural verb 'gather.' 'Gathers,' 'is gathering,' and 'has gathered' are all singular forms.

questions.passage: When Harrowgate Instruments introduced an inexpensive electronic keyboard, the company advertised it as an affordable substitute for the piano and the organ, able to imitate their sounds at a fraction of the cost. ______ some musicians soon came to value the keyboard for the very qualities that made it a poor imitation: its thin, reedy tones and a faint buzz that no acoustic instrument could produce.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Ironically,
Accordingly,
Likewise,
In short,
questions.explanation: The keyboard was sold as a convincing imitation, yet musicians prized it for failing to be one, an unexpected reversal that 'Ironically' captures. 'Accordingly' (B) would make the musicians' taste a logical result of the advertising; 'Likewise' (C) signals similarity and 'In short' (D) a summary.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith.
• He created a written form of the Cherokee language called a syllabary.
• In a syllabary, each character represents a syllable rather than a single sound.
• Sequoyah completed the syllabary in 1821.
• Within a few years, thousands of Cherokee people had learned to read and write with it.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how quickly the syllabary was adopted. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Sequoyah's syllabary, completed in 1821, is a writing system in which each character represents a syllable.
Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith, created a written form of the Cherokee language.
Within a few years of Sequoyah's completing it in 1821, thousands of Cherokee people had learned to read and write with the syllabary.
In the Cherokee syllabary, each character represents a syllable rather than a single sound.
questions.explanation: Only choice C conveys speed, pairing the completion date with the thousands who learned the system 'within a few years.' Choice A gives the date but not the adoption, and B and D describe Sequoyah and the writing system.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Several cities have experimented with making buses free to ride. Transportation analyst Soraya Mbeki-Hart argues that eliminating fares is the most effective way to persuade drivers to switch to public transit, since cost is the reason people most often give for not riding.

Text 2
When the city of Wexley eliminated bus fares, ridership rose by about 20 percent in the first year. But surveys found that most new riders had previously walked or cycled, and the share of trips made by car barely changed. Residents who continued to drive mostly cited infrequent service, not cost, as their reason.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Mbeki-Hart's argument in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that eliminating fares both increases ridership and reduces car trips.
By arguing that bus fares should be raised to pay for more frequent service.
By noting that eliminating fares in Wexley increased ridership but did little to draw drivers out of their cars.
By questioning whether surveys of transit riders can be trusted.
questions.explanation: Text 2 grants that ridership rose but shows that new riders came mainly from walking and cycling while car trips barely changed, so free buses did little to win over drivers. Choice A ignores that evidence; D contradicts Text 2's own reliance on surveys; B is a proposal Text 2 never makes.

questions.passage:
Pottery Fragments from Three Layers at the Port of Nemara

Layer (approx. date)  Total sherds  Imported sherds  Share imported
Layer 3 (700 BCE)     1,200         96               8%
Layer 2 (600 BCE)     800           120              15%
Layer 1 (500 BCE)     2,000         160              8%

Archaeologist Yetunde Carrasco argues that Nemara's overseas trade peaked around 600 BCE. She cautions that raw counts of imported pottery can mislead, because far more pottery was recovered from some layers than from others, and she notes that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: although Layer 1 contained the most imported sherds, imported pottery made up a larger share of the sherds in Layer 2 than in either other layer.
Layer 1 contained 160 imported sherds, more than either of the other layers.
Layer 3 and Layer 1 had the same share of imported sherds, 8%.
Layer 2 yielded fewer total sherds than either of the other layers.
questions.explanation: Carrasco warns that raw counts mislead, so the relevant measure is the share of imported sherds. Choice A shows that Layer 2 (600 BCE) has the highest share even though Layer 1 has the most imported sherds. Choice B relies on the raw count she warns against; C and D do not point to a peak at 600 BCE.

questions.passage: Why does a cut apple turn brown? When the fruit's cells are damaged, an enzyme inside them comes into contact with oxygen from the air and triggers reactions that produce brown pigments. A squeeze of lemon juice slows the browning, in part because the juice's acidity interferes with the enzyme's activity.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that lemon juice is the best way to keep fruit fresh.
To compare the browning of apples with that of other fruits.
To warn readers that browned apples are unsafe to eat.
To explain the chemical cause of a familiar change and why one remedy works.
questions.explanation: The text asks why cut apples brown, answers with the enzyme-oxygen reaction, and explains why lemon juice slows it. It does not claim lemon juice is best (A), discuss other fruits (B), or say that browned apples are unsafe (C).

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story.

When the class election results were posted, Mateo congratulated Rin with a grin so wide and a handshake so vigorous that everyone agreed he was taking the loss well. Only Rin, who had known him since kindergarten, noticed that his enthusiasm was a little too ______, the performance of a good sport rather than the feeling of one.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: sincere
studied
subdued
spontaneous
questions.explanation: 'Studied' means deliberate or carefully practiced, which fits Rin's sense that the enthusiasm is 'the performance of a good sport rather than the feeling of one.' 'Sincere' and 'spontaneous' are the opposite of a performance, and 'subdued' contradicts the wide grin and vigorous handshake.

questions.passage: Archaeologists long assumed that the stone weights found at the ancient market town of Qaredh were made for local use, since they were cut from limestone, a common stone found throughout the region. But when researcher Wanjiru Holmberg measured the weights, she found that their masses matched a standard unit used at ports far to the south, not the unit recorded in Qaredh's own inscriptions. Holmberg suggests that merchants from those ports carried their own weights with them, measuring goods by the standards of their home markets.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Evidence from the weights' masses suggests that some weights at Qaredh belonged to merchants from distant ports rather than to the town's own traders.
The limestone used for Qaredh's weights could only have come from quarries far to the south.
Qaredh's inscriptions record the prices of goods sold at its market.
Merchants at Qaredh were required to use the town's official unit of weight.
questions.explanation: The text overturns an assumption about the weights: their masses match a southern standard, so Holmberg concludes they belonged to visiting merchants. Choice B contradicts the statement that limestone is common throughout the region, and it confuses the stone with the unit of weight; D contradicts Holmberg's conclusion; C is not stated.

questions.passage: When the city of Hollin replaced several parking lots near its central train station with apartment buildings, some downtown business owners warned that shoppers would stop coming downtown. A study two years later found that downtown sales had risen slightly and that most shoppers surveyed had arrived by train or on foot rather than by car. These results suggest that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the new apartment buildings were built mainly for people who work at the train station.
Hollin should remove every remaining parking lot in the city.
shoppers who drive downtown spend more per visit than shoppers who arrive by train.
removing the parking lots did not drive shoppers away from downtown, as some business owners had feared.
questions.explanation: Sales rose after the lots were removed, and most shoppers arrived without cars, so the feared loss of shoppers did not happen. Choice B is a sweeping recommendation the text does not support, and A and C introduce claims the study does not address.

questions.passage: Bronze—an alloy of copper and ______ is considerably harder than pure copper, a property that made it valuable to ancient metalworkers who produced tools, weapons, and fittings for ships.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: tin,
tin
tin—
tin;
questions.explanation: The phrase 'an alloy of copper and tin' interrupts the sentence and is opened with a dash, so it must be closed with a matching dash before the verb 'is.' A comma (A) cannot close a dash-opened phrase; no punctuation (B) leaves it open; a semicolon (D) would cut the subject off from its verb.

questions.passage: Every afternoon during the school year, Soledad and her friend Joaquin ______ younger students with their math homework at the long tables in the back of the school library.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: helps
help
has helped
is helping
questions.explanation: The compound subject 'Soledad and her friend Joaquin' is plural, so it takes the plural verb 'help.' 'Helps,' 'has helped,' and 'is helping' are all singular forms.

questions.passage: Vulcanized rubber is far more durable than natural rubber: heating rubber with sulfur links its long molecules together, so the material no longer turns sticky in heat or brittle in cold. ______ those same links make vulcanized rubber hard to recycle, since it cannot simply be melted down and reshaped.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: That said,
In other words,
Specifically,
Likewise,
questions.explanation: The first sentence praises vulcanized rubber's durability; the second names a drawback caused by the same molecular links, so a concessive transition, 'that said,' fits. 'In other words' and 'specifically' would introduce a restatement or detail of the praise, and 'likewise' would add a similar advantage.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The city of Quennell opened a bike-share program in 2018.
• The program began with 40 stations and 300 bicycles.
• By 2023 it had grown to 120 stations and 1,100 bicycles.
• Riders can unlock a bicycle with their transit card.
• Most trips last less than 20 minutes.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how much Quennell's bike-share program grew. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Riders in Quennell can unlock a share bicycle with their transit card.
Most trips in Quennell's bike-share program last less than 20 minutes.
Quennell's bike-share program opened in 2018 with 40 stations.
Quennell's bike-share program grew from 40 stations and 300 bicycles in 2018 to 120 stations and 1,100 bicycles by 2023.
questions.explanation: Growth requires a before-and-after comparison, and choice D gives both the starting and later numbers. Choice C gives only the starting size, and A and B describe how the program is used.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Film archivist Beatriz Onwuachi-Holm argues that the goal of restoring an old film should be to let modern audiences see it as its first audiences did. Scratches, dust, and flicker, she notes, are damage that built up over decades of projection and storage; removing them returns the film to its original state.

Text 2
Digital tools can now erase almost any blemish from an old film, and restorers are tempted to use them freely. But the grain of the original film stock was never damage: it was part of how the picture looked on opening night. Restorers who smooth it away along with the scratches produce an image cleaner than any the first audiences ever saw.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Onwuachi-Holm's argument in Text 1?
choices: By accepting her goal but warning that pursuing it carelessly can remove features that were part of the original film.
By arguing that scratches and flicker should be preserved because they record a film's history.
By rejecting the idea that a restored film should look the way it did for its first audiences.
By claiming that digital tools cannot reliably remove scratches and dust.
questions.explanation: Text 2 judges over-cleaned films by Onwuachi-Holm's own standard (what 'first audiences' saw), so it shares her goal while warning that grain is not damage and should not be removed. It does not defend scratches (B), reject the goal (C), or doubt the tools' power (D).

questions.passage:
Algae Cover on Three Types of Reef Plots, Tessaly Reef

Plot type                  Month 0  Month 6
Full cage (fish kept out)  12%      58%
Partial cage (fish enter)  11%      15%
Open plot                  13%      14%

To test whether grazing fish keep algae in check, marine ecologist Njeri Castellanos covered some reef plots with cages that kept fish out, left others open, and covered a third set with partial cages, which had a roof but open sides. Partial cages shade a plot much as full cages do but let fish in. Castellanos concluded that the loss of grazing fish, not the cage structure itself, explained the change in the fully caged plots, noting that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: algae cover in the fully caged plots rose from 12% to 58% over six months.
algae cover in the open plots changed by only one percentage point over six months.
algae cover rose sharply in the fully caged plots but barely changed in the partially caged plots, which also had cage structures but let fish in.
all three types of plots began the study with similar algae cover, between 11% and 13%.
questions.explanation: To separate the effect of losing fish from the effect of the cage, the full cages must be compared with the partial cages, which share the structure but admit fish; choice C makes that comparison. A and B each describe one plot type, and D gives only the similar starting values.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story.

The old tractor had not started on the first try in eleven years. It coughed, it shuddered, it released a cloud of black smoke that sent the hens running, and then, just when anyone else would have given up, it caught. Mr. Haddad always patted the hood afterward, the way a person might thank a stubborn old friend for coming through one more time.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why Mr. Haddad cannot afford to replace his tractor.
To portray Mr. Haddad's affectionate relationship with an unreliable old tractor.
To describe the effect of the tractor's smoke on the farm's animals.
To show that Mr. Haddad is frustrated by the time the tractor wastes each morning.
questions.explanation: The text describes the tractor's struggles and ends with Mr. Haddad patting it like 'a stubborn old friend,' conveying fondness. D contradicts that fondness; A is never mentioned, and C is a passing detail.

questions.passage: Psychologist Yusra Kallström found that a person's confidence in a memory is a ______ guide to its accuracy: participants who described a memory as 'crystal clear' were wrong about its details nearly as often as those who described it as 'hazy.'
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: dependable
revealing
deliberate
fallible
questions.explanation: Confident and unconfident participants were wrong about equally often, so confidence is a fallible, or unreliable, guide. 'Dependable' and 'revealing' say the opposite; 'deliberate' does not describe a guide's accuracy.

questions.passage: When a whale dies and sinks to the deep seafloor, its carcass can sustain a series of communities for decades: scavengers strip the flesh, small worms and crustaceans colonize the surrounding sediment, and finally bacteria break down the fats inside the bones. Marine biologist Selu Fonoti argues that such 'whale falls' are not isolated curiosities. Because great whales were once far more numerous, she reasons, their carcasses would have been scattered across the ocean floor closely enough to serve as stepping stones, letting species that depend on them spread across entire ocean basins. The hunting that reduced whale populations may therefore have affected life far below the surface.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Whale carcasses on the seafloor are consumed in a fixed order, beginning with scavengers and ending with bacteria.
Deep-sea species that feed on whale carcasses have gone extinct since whale populations declined.
A researcher proposes that whale carcasses once connected deep-sea habitats across oceans, so the decline of whales may have had far-reaching effects on deep-sea life.
Whale hunting was the main cause of the decline of deep-sea ecosystems.
questions.explanation: The text's focus is Fonoti's argument that abundant carcasses once linked deep-sea communities and that whaling may therefore have affected them. A is only the opening background; B and D turn her cautious 'may' into definite claims the text does not make.

questions.passage: In the first years of sound film, microphones were bulky and had to stay in fixed positions, and the noisy cameras were shut inside soundproof booths so that their whirring would not be recorded. Film historians have observed that many movies from those years look stiffer and more static than the silent films made just a few years earlier. Taken together, these points suggest that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the technical demands of recording sound limited how freely early sound films could move the camera and position actors.
audiences preferred silent films to sound films once both were widely available.
most actors from silent films were unable to adapt to speaking roles.
early microphones recorded sound more clearly than the microphones used later.
questions.explanation: Fixed microphones and cameras sealed in booths would restrict movement, which accounts for the stiffness historians observe. B and C offer explanations the text never mentions, and D is unsupported.

questions.passage: The leatherback, which, unlike other sea turtles, lacks a hard ______ is covered instead by a layer of tough, oily skin stretched over a mosaic of small bones.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: shell
shell;
shell—
shell,
questions.explanation: The clause 'which, unlike other sea turtles, lacks a hard shell' is nonessential and opens with a comma, so a comma must close it before the main verb 'is.' A dash (C) would not match the opening comma, a semicolon (B) cannot separate a subject from its verb, and no punctuation (A) leaves the clause unclosed.

questions.passage: When the photographer finally developed the roll of film from her trip, she discovered that the camera's shutter ______ open the entire time, so every frame was a blank white rectangle.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: sticks
had stuck
will stick
is sticking
questions.explanation: The shutter's sticking happened before the past-tense discovery ('she discovered'), so the past perfect 'had stuck' is needed. The present and future forms do not fit a narrative set in the past.

questions.passage: Most people who resolve to start a new habit expect the first few days to be the hardest. Psychologist Lionel Okonjo found something different: among the participants he followed, consistency was high in the first week, when motivation was strong, and dropped most sharply in the third and fourth weeks. ______ he advises people building a habit to plan for extra support once the novelty wears off, not only at the start.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Accordingly,
Nevertheless,
For example,
Previously,
questions.explanation: The advice follows from the finding that the drop comes weeks in, so 'Accordingly' fits. 'Nevertheless' would set the advice against the finding, 'For example' treats it as an instance, and 'Previously' misstates the time order.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived.
• Adult blue whales can grow to about 30 meters (roughly 100 feet) long.
• Blue whales feed mainly on krill, tiny shrimp-like animals.
• They filter krill from seawater using baleen plates in their mouths.
• An adult blue whale can eat several tons of krill in a single day.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize the contrast between the size of blue whales and the size of their food. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Blue whales filter krill from seawater using baleen plates in their mouths.
An adult blue whale can eat several tons of krill in a single day.
Although blue whales, the largest animals known to have ever lived, can grow to about 30 meters long, they feed mainly on tiny shrimp-like animals called krill.
Adult blue whales can grow to about 30 meters (roughly 100 feet) long.
questions.explanation: A contrast in size needs both the whale's size and the food's; only choice C gives both. D gives the whale's size alone, and A and B describe feeding without contrasting sizes.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Food historian Marguerite Osei argues that the spread of home refrigeration in the twentieth century eroded many regional food traditions. Techniques such as pickling, smoking, and fermenting, she contends, survived for centuries because they were needed to keep food through the winter; once cold storage made them unnecessary, the knowledge behind them began to disappear.

Text 2
It is true that fewer households now preserve food out of necessity. But many preserved foods have outlived the need that created them. In regions where fermented vegetables or cured fish were once winter staples, cooks continue to prepare them because families have come to prize their flavors and to associate them with holidays and gatherings. Necessity may explain how such traditions began without explaining why they last.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Osei's argument in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that preservation techniques have largely vanished from the regions where they were once common.
By arguing that refrigeration has had little effect on how often households preserve food.
By suggesting that Osei treats these traditions as depending on necessity alone, overlooking other reasons people continue them.
By claiming that techniques such as pickling were first developed for their flavor rather than to keep food through the winter.
questions.explanation: Text 2 grants that necessity has declined but argues that flavor and association with gatherings keep the traditions alive, which Osei's necessity-based account overlooks. Choice D contradicts Text 2's statement that necessity 'may explain how such traditions began'; B contradicts its opening concession.

questions.passage: Botanist Kofi Adjei hypothesizes that a species of wild strawberry in a mountain meadow reproduces mainly by runners, horizontal stems that take root to form new plants, rather than by seed, and that as a result, strawberry plants growing close together in the meadow are usually genetically identical.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Adjei's hypothesis?
choices: Genetic tests showed that most clusters of strawberry plants growing within a few meters of one another in the meadow consisted of plants with identical DNA.
Strawberry plants in the meadow produced fewer fruits than strawberry plants of the same species in a nearby valley.
Birds that visit the meadow eat strawberry fruits and scatter the seeds over long distances.
The runners of strawberry plants in the meadow grew to an average length of about 30 centimeters.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis predicts that neighboring plants will be genetically identical, and choice A confirms that prediction. Choice D shows only that runners exist, not that they are the main means of reproduction; C points toward spread by seed and would weaken the hypothesis.

questions.passage: The wheelbarrow may seem too ordinary to be called an invention, yet it changed how people move heavy loads. A worker carrying a sack of soil must hold up its entire weight. With a wheelbarrow, the wheel bears much of the load, and the worker lifts and steers only a fraction of it. As a result, one person can move far more material in a day than by carrying it.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To trace the history of the wheelbarrow's invention.
To argue that the wheelbarrow should be replaced by more modern tools.
To compare the wheelbarrow with other simple machines.
To explain how an ordinary tool makes it easier to move heavy loads.
questions.explanation: The text explains that the wheel carries much of the weight, so a worker can move more material. It gives no dates or inventor (A), mentions no other machines (C), and praises the tool rather than calling for its replacement (B).

questions.passage: In the fishing villages that anthropologist Lucía Benavides studied, the first catch of each season is never sold. Instead, it is divided among every household, including those with no fishers of their own. Benavides argues that the custom is not merely ______: by guaranteeing each family a share of food at the start of the season, it gives real support to households that might otherwise go without.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: practical
ceremonial
profitable
competitive
questions.explanation: The colon contrasts the custom's ritual side with the real, material support it provides, so the custom is 'not merely ceremonial.' 'Practical' (A) cannot be right, because the real support described after the colon is itself a practical benefit; 'profitable' contradicts the fact that the catch is never sold, and nothing suggests the custom is 'competitive.'

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story. The narrator is returning to the town where she grew up after many years abroad.

The bus let me off where the fountain used to be. It had been replaced by a flat stone plaza, and the bakery on the corner now sold shoes. I stood with my suitcase and tried to feel something like arrival. Then a boy ran past with a paper cone of roasted chestnuts, and the smell—burnt sugar and woodsmoke—reached me before he did. I was nine again, counting coins at the vendor's cart, and for a moment the plaza did not matter at all.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The narrator is disappointed by how the town has changed and decides to leave.
Although the changed town at first feels unfamiliar, a familiar smell briefly reconnects the narrator with her childhood there.
The narrator comes to prefer the new stone plaza to the fountain she remembers.
The narrator regrets the years she spent abroad and wishes she had never left.
questions.explanation: The narrator cannot 'feel something like arrival' amid the changes until the smell of chestnuts returns her to age nine. Choice C misreads 'the plaza did not matter at all,' which means the plaza stopped troubling her, not that she prefers it; A and D are not supported.

questions.passage: Many desert plants open their pores, called stomata, only at night, when the air is cooler and more humid. They take in carbon dioxide through the open pores and store it in a chemical form until daylight, when they use it in photosynthesis. Keeping the pores closed during the heat of the day greatly reduces the amount of water the plants lose. This adaptation is therefore especially useful for plants that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: grow in shady rainforests where rain falls almost every day.
flower only at night.
need unusually large amounts of carbon dioxide.
grow where water is scarce and daytime temperatures are high.
questions.explanation: The adaptation's benefit is saving water during hot days, so it helps most where water is scarce and days are hot. Choice A describes the opposite conditions; B confuses when the pores open with when the plants flower, and C is not supported.

questions.passage: The engineer who designed the valley's first suspension ______ had never built anything longer than a barn before taking on the project, yet her bridge carried traffic across the river for more than sixty years.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: bridge
bridge,
bridge;
bridge:
questions.explanation: 'The engineer who designed the valley's first suspension bridge' is the subject, and 'had never built' is its verb; no punctuation should separate them. A comma (B), semicolon (C), or colon (D) would wrongly split the subject from its verb.

questions.passage: Among the dishes prepared for the village's spring festival ______ a flatbread stuffed with wild greens, which families gather from the surrounding hills on the morning of the celebration.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: are
have been
is
were
questions.explanation: The sentence is inverted: its subject is 'a flatbread,' which comes after the verb and is singular, so 'is' is required. The plural choices agree with 'dishes,' which is part of the opening prepositional phrase and cannot be the subject.

questions.passage: Young sunflower plants often turn their heads to follow the sun across the sky, facing east in the morning and west by evening. ______ once the flowers are fully open, most heads stop moving and stay facing east.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: However,
For example,
Therefore,
Similarly,
questions.explanation: Mature flowers stop moving, in contrast to the young plants that track the sun, so 'however' fits. 'For example' (B) would present the second sentence as an instance of sun-tracking, which it is not; 'therefore' and 'similarly' also misstate the relationship.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Injera is a flatbread eaten widely in Ethiopia and Eritrea.
• It is traditionally made from teff, a tiny grain native to the Ethiopian highlands.
• The batter is left to ferment for several days before cooking, giving injera a slightly sour taste.
• Stews and vegetables are served on top of a large round of injera.
• Diners tear off pieces of injera to scoop up the food.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize that injera serves more than one purpose during a meal. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Injera is traditionally made from teff, a tiny grain native to the Ethiopian highlands.
Injera's batter ferments for several days before cooking, which gives the bread a slightly sour taste.
Injera, a flatbread made from teff, is eaten widely in Ethiopia and Eritrea.
Injera is both plate and utensil: stews and vegetables are served on top of a large round of it, and diners tear off pieces to scoop up the food.
questions.explanation: Choice D shows injera doing two jobs at a meal, holding the food and serving to scoop it. A and C describe its ingredients and where it is eaten, and B its preparation, none of which conveys more than one use.

questions.passage: Director Soledad Ferrante's revival of the comedy changed none of its dialogue, yet her staging was hardly ______: by moving the action from an elegant drawing room to a crowded train station, she altered how nearly every line would be understood.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: inventive
abridged
deferential
elaborate
questions.explanation: Keeping every line suggests respect for the original, but 'yet... hardly' introduces the opposite: the new setting transformed the play, so it was hardly deferential. 'Inventive' is what the staging actually was, so 'hardly inventive' contradicts the text, and 'abridged' would not contrast with keeping all the dialogue.

questions.passage: Snowflakes are often said to be unique, and in a sense they are: each forms along its own path through a cloud, meeting slightly different temperatures and humidity as it grows. Yet those same conditions also explain why snowflakes fall into recognizable types. Physicist Mireille Onwuachi has shown in laboratory chambers that ice crystals grown at about −2°C tend to form thin, flat plates, while those grown near −5°C form long needles, so flakes that grew under similar conditions share a basic shape.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence?
choices: It introduces a qualification to the idea that every snowflake is unique, which the rest of the text develops.
It restates the claim made in the first sentence in different terms.
It presents a hypothesis that Onwuachi's experiments later disproved.
It explains why snowflakes can form only at certain temperatures.
questions.explanation: 'Yet' turns from uniqueness to the recognizable types that snowflakes share, a point Onwuachi's findings then support. Choice C reverses the relationship: the experiments support the sentence rather than disprove it.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Many dance teachers ask beginning students to practice in front of mirrors, reasoning that dancers who can see their own movements can correct errors in alignment and timing immediately. Dance educator Priya Castellanos argues that the mirror is among the most valuable tools a beginning dancer has.

Text 2
In a study by kinesiologist Aarav Lindgren, two groups of beginning dancers learned the same routine, one with mirrors and one without. Right after the lessons, the mirror group performed slightly better. A week later, however, when both groups were tested in a room without mirrors, the group that had practiced without them performed the routine more accurately, apparently because those dancers had learned to rely on their own sense of where their bodies were.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Castellanos's argument?
choices: By agreeing that mirrors help beginning dancers remember routines over time.
By suggesting that the immediate benefits of practicing with mirrors may come at the cost of dancers' ability to perform without them later.
By arguing that beginning dancers should not learn routines until they have developed good alignment.
By claiming that mirrors make it harder for dancers to correct errors during practice.
questions.explanation: Text 2 reports that the mirror group did better at first but worse a week later without mirrors, which complicates Castellanos's praise. Choice D contradicts Text 2, which found the mirror group performing better right after practice.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story. Tomasz has lived alone in his apartment since his daughter, Ania, moved to another city.

The plant on the windowsill had been Ania's. She had left it behind with a note, water on Sundays, and Tomasz followed the instruction so exactly that he sometimes felt foolish, standing at the sink with the little blue watering can at nine o'clock each Sunday as if someone were checking. The plant did not seem to care much either way. It grew slowly, leaning toward the glass. Still, when Ania called and asked, as she always did, how it was doing, he found that he had a great deal to say.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Tomasz resents having to care for a plant he never wanted.
Tomasz is unsure how to keep the plant healthy.
The plant is thriving because of Tomasz's careful attention.
Tomasz's devoted care of the plant serves partly as a way of staying connected to his daughter.
questions.explanation: Tomasz follows Ania's note exactly and has 'a great deal to say' when she asks about the plant, so caring for it keeps him close to her. His feeling 'foolish' is self-consciousness, not resentment (A), and the plant 'did not seem to care much,' which rules out C.

questions.passage:
Average Number of Foggy Days per Year at Four Coastal Weather Stations

Station         Distance from shore (km)  Foggy days
Harwick Point   0.5                       94
Selby Cove      2                         71
Ormond Ridge    8                         40
Tallis Flats    15                        18

A meteorology student claims that, at these four stations, fog is less frequent farther from the shore. She supports the claim by noting that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Harwick Point, the station closest to shore, averages 94 foggy days per year, while Tallis Flats, the station farthest from shore, averages only 18.
Selby Cove averages 71 foggy days per year.
Ormond Ridge is 8 kilometers from shore.
Harwick Point and Selby Cove together average 165 foggy days per year.
questions.explanation: The claim links distance to fog frequency, so the support must pair the two; choice A compares the nearest and farthest stations. Choices B and C each give only one measure for one station.

questions.passage: A string stretched between two posts on a board produces only a faint sound when plucked, because a thin string pushes very little air as it vibrates. An acoustic guitar solves this problem with its hollow body: the vibrating strings set the guitar's thin wooden top vibrating, and because the top is light and flexible, its broad surface moves far more air than the strings could alone. It follows that a solid, heavy block of wood shaped like a guitar and fitted with the same strings would most likely ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: produce a louder sound than an acoustic guitar, because it contains more wood.
cause its strings to vibrate more slowly than those of an acoustic guitar.
produce a much fainter sound than an acoustic guitar, since its rigid surface would move relatively little air.
be easier to keep in tune than an acoustic guitar.
questions.explanation: The text credits the guitar's volume to a light, flexible top that vibrates and moves air; a heavy, rigid block could not do so, so it would sound faint. Choice A assumes the amount of wood matters, but the text says the top's lightness and flexibility are what matter.

questions.passage: After months of public comment, the town's election committee issued a report recommending three changes: moving the District 2 polling place to the public ______ a larger building with more parking; extending voting hours by one hour in the evening; and adding a second ballot drop box downtown.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: library;
library,
library:
library
questions.explanation: 'A larger building with more parking' describes the library and belongs to the first item, so a comma sets it off; semicolons separate the three items because the first contains a comma. A semicolon (A) would make the description a separate fourth item, contradicting 'three changes'; a colon (C) cannot introduce a description inside a list that a colon already introduces, and no punctuation (D) runs the description into 'library.'

questions.passage: For the spring showcase, the members of the Riverside Youth Dance Troupe ______ their own costumes over the winter, sewing hundreds of sequins onto each one by hand.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: designs
is designing
designed
has designed
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural 'members,' so the verb must be plural, and 'designed' is the only plural-compatible choice. 'Designs,' 'is designing,' and 'has designed' agree with the singular 'troupe,' which is inside a prepositional phrase.

questions.passage: Stage actors are often taught to 'cheat out,' angling their bodies partly toward the audience even while speaking to another character. Critics of the practice say it looks unnatural, and they have a point. ______ people in real conversations turn to face each other. But a play is not a real conversation: an actor who fully faced a scene partner would hide half of her face, and much of her voice, from the audience.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Instead,
Consequently,
Meanwhile,
After all,
questions.explanation: The sentence gives the reason the critics 'have a point,' and 'after all' introduces such a supporting reason. 'Consequently' would wrongly present how people converse as a result of the critics' complaint.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• A town meeting is a form of local government in which a town's voters gather to debate and decide local laws and budgets directly.
• Town meetings are used in many small towns in New England.
• In a town meeting, any registered voter of the town who attends may speak and vote.
• In most other U.S. cities and towns, voters elect representatives, such as council members, who make these decisions.
questions.stem: The student wants to contrast town meetings with the way most U.S. cities and towns make local decisions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Whereas voters in most U.S. cities and towns elect representatives to decide local laws and budgets, voters at a town meeting debate and decide these matters directly.
Town meetings, in which voters debate and decide local laws and budgets, are used in many small New England towns.
In a town meeting, any registered voter of the town who attends may speak and vote.
In most U.S. cities and towns, voters elect representatives, such as council members, to make decisions about local laws and budgets.
questions.explanation: A contrast needs both systems, and only choice A sets elected representatives against direct decision-making. Choice D describes only the representative system, and B and C describe only town meetings.

questions.passage: Obsidian, a natural volcanic glass, forms when lava cools too quickly for crystals to grow. Because the glass breaks ______, leaving smooth, curved surfaces and edges sharper than those of a steel blade, early toolmakers in many parts of the world prized it for knives and arrowheads.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: unpredictably
cleanly
rarely
slowly
questions.explanation: Smooth surfaces and razor-sharp edges are the marks of a clean break, which is what made obsidian useful for blades. 'Unpredictably' would make the stone hard to shape into tools rather than prized for them; 'rarely' and 'slowly' say nothing about the smooth, sharp result.

questions.passage: When the pianoforte was developed in Italy around 1700, its name announced what set it apart from the harpsichord. A harpsichord plucks its strings with nearly the same force no matter how a key is pressed, but the new instrument let players make notes soft ('piano') or loud ('forte') by ______ how firmly they struck the keys.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: ignoring
concealing
repeating
varying
questions.explanation: Players made notes soft or loud by changing the force of their touch, which is the contrast with the harpsichord; 'varying' says exactly that. 'Ignoring' how firmly the keys are struck describes the harpsichord, not the new instrument, and 'concealing' and 'repeating' do not fit.

questions.passage: Many meteor showers return at about the same time every year. As comets travel around the Sun, they shed trails of dust and small rocky particles. When Earth's orbit carries the planet through one of these trails, the particles strike the atmosphere at high speed and burn up, producing streaks of light. Because Earth crosses the same trails at the same point in its orbit each year, these showers can be predicted well in advance.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Many meteor showers recur on a predictable schedule because Earth passes through the same comet debris at the same point in its yearly orbit.
Comets shed more dust the closer they travel to the Sun.
Meteor showers are best viewed from places far from city lights.
Most particles shed by comets are too small to be seen from Earth.
questions.explanation: The text explains what causes meteor showers and why many of them return each year, ending on their predictability. Choices B and D add claims the text does not make, and C is not discussed.

questions.passage: The rock at the summit of Mount Everest is limestone that formed from sediment on the floor of an ancient ______ over millions of years, the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates lifted that rock more than eight kilometers above sea level.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: sea,
sea
sea;
sea, then
questions.explanation: The text contains two independent clauses ('The rock... ancient sea' and 'over millions of years, the collision... lifted that rock'), so a semicolon can join them. A comma alone (A) creates a comma splice, as does a comma followed by 'then' (D), and no punctuation (B) creates a run-on sentence.
